subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF ENFORCEMENT OF AIR SAFETY REGULATIONS- CALL FOR MINISTER'S RESIGNATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. It arises from a news story by Tom VanDusen in today's Ottawa Citizen in which he quotes a government task force report that "enforcement of Canada's air safety regulations is generally unco-ordinated and often haphazard".

That this House calls for the immediate resignation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and calls upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to order an immediate inquiry into all aspects of air safety.

THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON CONSUMER PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who, as we all know, has spoken very fondly of his falling dollar.
Can he tell the House today some of the consequences of the fall in our dollar, consequences in respect of consumers in Canada? In particular, would the minister indicate to the House whether he is aware that beef is now selling in Omaha for $64 per hundredweight and the same type of beef is selling wholesale in Toronto for $78 to $80 per hundredweight, with the main difference between the two prices resulting from the discounted Canadian dollar?
If the minister is aware of this, would he indicate to the House whether or not his department has done any study to determine the effect of Canadian-produced beef on consumer prices in Canada and, if so, could he tell the House what that study shows?

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: DEVALUED CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON CONSUMER PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said in committee this morning that I was well aware that the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, while providing many benefits on the production side and the export side, has had some bad side-effects on the inflationary side of the economy. I have said many times that it is not unexpected, when there is devaluation of a country's currency, to suffer price increases due in many cases to prices established on international markets. I do not deny that the government is preoccupied with this matter.
I believe that the effect of beef prices on production in Canada, however, is not only related to the devaluation of the dollar. Many people are of the opinion-and there is some truth to it-that perhaps beef prices were too low some years ago and, as a result, herds were depleted. Producers are in the process of rebuilding their herds and, of course, if prices are higher it helps those producers to achieve a better production level.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member forgets to mention that the consumer price index went down from 9.8 per cent in July to 8.4 per cent last month. The CPI is the composite indicator of all price levels in Canada.
I said in October of 1977 that we would end the controls and that we should have confidence in the marketplace, and in the speech I made in Toronto on Monday I said that everyone will have to fulfil his responsibilities. I said that I am not against profits but that profits should be used to reduce prices or be reinvested in productive capacity in order to increase it and to make Canadian goods more competitive on world markets. A substantial decline in the value of the Canadian dollar relative to the United States dollar had become inevitable because of the higher rate of price and cost inflation in Canada than in the United States earlier in the 1970s.
The minister's party was in power then and it is in power now. If that was true in the earlier part of the 1970s, is it not also true that if we have a higher rate of price and cost inflation this year, we will be in great difficulties again? It is at this moment, and that is why I made that speech urging all Canadians to show restraint and responsibility so that we can keep our faith in the marketplace and let the market

forces decide the levels. However, everyone will have to show responsibility and restraint if we want to achieve our goal.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because some 24 per cent of the oil Canada imports comes from Iran, and since there has been very little production for months and not much indication that there will be a resumption of supply in the immediate future, would the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources share with the House his assessment of the situation and tell us what steps Canada is taking to replace this oil and to decrease our dependency upon oil from Iran?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
maintopic: DOMESTIC OIL. PRODUCTION-STEPS TO DECREASE DEPENDENCY ON IRAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have indicated in recent answers that the situation is a serious one and that there might well be shortages affecting eastern refineries. The corporation which owns these refineries has been making plans, running down its storage and inventories and making other arrangements for shipments. For example, a very substantial shipment arrived in Port Tupper today from Kuwait.
The most promising prospect, in my view, has to do with exchanges involving Canadian oil which would be moved through the Canadian system to Chicago, replacing oil which would otherwise be brought up to that city from the United States east coast. Instead of going to Chicago through the United States system, that oil would go to Canadian ports and refineries. I believe arrangements concerning something in the order of a million barrels have already been approved by the National Energy Board, and there may be applications involving as many as three million barrels under these exchange arrangements. subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-ECONOMIC COUNCIL OF CANADA STUDY- STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
MR. BROADBENT-ECONOMIC COUNCIL OF CANADA STUDY- STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising from answers given earlier today during oral questions by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). The minister said two things which are quite disturbing.
I made reference to a study produced by the Economic Council of Canada in which it documented what was claimed to have been excess profits in the period 1968 to 1973. Obviously I do not have the words of the Minister of Finance written down, but I am sure I can convey the accurate sense of what he said earlier today. He implied that the study had been repudiated by the Economic Council of Canada, and that an official disclaimer had been issued by the Economic Council of Canada. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, the minister was casting severe criticism on Professor Mintz who spent more than three years doing a study requested by the Government of Canada.
Would the minister confirm that it is the standard practice of the Economic Council of Canada, when a study is released in the name of one individual, to issue such a disclaimer? That is the standard practice. It is not exceptional for the Economic Council of Canada to make clear that a report is issued in the name of an individual. Surely the crucial point is that when the council makes such a statement, it is not dissociating itself
Privilege-Mr. Broadbent
from the findings. It is simply indicating that one individual did the work. If the minister is referring only to the standard disclaimer, it is an understatement to say I find it disagreeable that aspersions should be cast on the quality of work of a man who worked almost three years for a government agency. If the minister is referring to a more specific disclaimer which calls into question the quality of work, I am not aware of it, and I hope he will clarify that.
My second point is equally serious. The minister indicated that I was using outdated statistics in my question. That is false as well. I am not saying that the minister deliberately misled the House; I am saying only that he misled the House. In my question I referred to current statistics which were derived from official reports produced by the companies themselves. I do not intend to read all the statistics, but I should like to refer to two statistics for the years 1977 and 1978. The profits of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank of Canada and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce for 1977 increased by 10.6 per cent, which was well above average. For the most recent year 1978, their profits were up 34.4 per cent to almost $1 billion. In short, the trend to which Professor Mintz referred in the earlier period has continued up to the present. The statistics I used were accurate and current ones, and I resent the implication that I was doing something to the contrary.

subtopic: MR. BROADBENT-ECONOMIC COUNCIL OF CANADA STUDY- STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I referred to the study, I was referring to the paragraph appearing on the first page which reads as follows:
The findings of this study are the personal responsibility of the author and, as such, have not been endorsed by members of the Economic Council of Canada.

maintopic: MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I gave Your Honour notice of a question of privilege which involves the refusal of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) to make available to myself and other concerned parties a written statement made by the minister and called a "clarifying memorandum". According to the minister's letter, apparently it was sent out to all offices of his department, including his regional officials.
The underlying facts can be stated very briefly regarding the so-called clarifying memorandum dealing with the admission and deportation of Chilean refugees.
An inter-church committee on human rights in Latin America, composed of representatives of the Roman Catholic, United, Anglican, Presbyterian and Lutheran churches, was anxious, in pursuance of its efforts to assist refugees of Chile, where terror and torture have been habitually used, to obtain copies of any directives issued by the minister's office bearing on this question of admission of refugees. I passed this request on to the deputy minister and to the minister, but no document was made available.
I can pass over the intermediate correspondence and say that on February 6 the minister wrote to me and said this clarifying memorandum, as he called it, was in fact sent out as an internal departmental document to regional offices, but the minister was not prepared, on the basis of a long-standing practice, to release an internal memorandum of this nature.
I point out to you first of all, Mr. Speaker, that the immigration policy by section 3 declares the policies of this parliament on immigration, and includes (g) which is to fulfil Canada's international legal obligations with respect to

refugees and to uphold its humanitarian tradition with respect to the displaced and the persecuted.
You will be aware, Mr. Speaker, as members of this House are aware, that the exercise of this power under the act to admit refugees is covered by a series of discretionary jurisdictions conferred on officials of the department, so that when the minister sends out a memorandum dealing with the matter he in fact is giving directives as to how this power shall be exercised. It is obvious, therefore, in effect, that the memorandum was a directive to officials as to how they should exercise their discretion in respect of allowing refugees either to come to Canada or stay in Canada.
I submit there is a clear case here of breach of privilege. As a member of this House I am deprived of the ability to review the memorandum and the decision, and to advise those who sought my advice on the matter. I submit that the action of the minister in refusing to make this document available to me and, presumably, to other members of the House and to those who sought it, namely, the committee of the churches to which I have referred, is contrary to the purposes of the act which refer to the humanitarian traditions of Canada. I submit that it is a deprivation of would-be immigrants' or refugees' basic rights and elementary justice. How can a refugee state his case under the various provisions set out in the act and the regulations unless he knows what instructions the officer examining him may happen to have in regard to admission?
Again I suggest this is a shocking disregard of the right of members of this House to know what is done in the name of this House in dealing with a statutory authority given by this House. The minister, under the pretence that this is an internal matter, refuses to disclose what is a general document issued for the instruction of his officials. I suggest that this action of the minister shows his insensitivity to the need for co-operation with voluntary organizations, such as the churches, in looking after this obligation of Canada in accordance with its humanitarian traditions.
Furthermore, this amounts to a breach of the promise made on behalf of the minister, with the minister present, to a committee of this House, the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, which was examining the act. On that occasion a Mr. Tait, who is an official of the department, was stating the view and interpretation of the act, and in the presence of members of the committee and the minister he said it had been decided that basic directives of the department would be made public. Instead of that, we have this policy of continued, blatant secrecy, all too common in this House.
I therefore urge on Your Honour that this is a prima facie case of privilege and, if you rule that it is, I would move that the minister be instructed to divulge this document. The House could then deal with the matter following your ruling.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
maintopic: MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
speechtext:
First and foremost, Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his courtesy in sending me a copy of the letter he wrote to you indicating he would be raising this question of privilege today.
February 8, 1979

I have reviewed all the correspondence with the hon. member leading up to his letter to you of February 7 in which he indicated he would be raising a question of privilege. Quite sincerely, 1 believe we have acted entirely properly in our responses to the hon. member, and that we have provided him with all the information relevant to his concerns. I will provide you, Mr. Speaker, with copies of the correspondence.
I would further suggest that this so-called question of privilege should more properly be put as a notice of motion for the production of papers.
On December 8, however, I wrote to the hon. member in response to his request to myself and my deputy minister and provided full information on our policy regarding deportation to Chile of persons whose claim to refugee status had been rejected by the refugee status advisory committee. In that letter, after acknowledging the questions he was asking in his earlier letter to me, I said this:
Our current procedure is that once the Immigration Appeal Board has confirmed our decision in those cases where this is applicable, the individual is allowed sixty days to leave Canada to a country of his choice. If the individual cannot or will not depart voluntarily to a third country, deportation to Chile is then carried out. However, the sixty-day period can be extended in those cases where approval to enter a third country seems imminent.
Where humanitarian conditions are found to exist, the individual will be permitted to remain in Canada and permanent status approved.
In summary, the commission has always carefully reviewed cases involving possible deportation to Chile. For some months in 1977-78 deportation was deferred in individual cases while additional information on the possibility of admission to a third country was obtained. In order to ensure a uniform understanding of the commission's position, as described above, a clarifying instruction was issued to all offices in September, 1978.
I gave the hon. member the full story so far as deportation to Chile is concerned, and the letter was based directly on an internal document, as I indicated to the hon. member. I indicated in the letter that there was nothing further to add to what I had put in my letter. Secondly, I made clear in my letters of both December 8 and February 6 that I did not myself issue any instruction or statement on this matter in August, 1978, or at any subsequent time.
I have been completely open and frank in providing the hon. member with information on this matter and do not believe his rights have in any way been infringed.
The hon. member raises a second question about a commitment made at the committee stage. In my letter of February 6 I commented on this as follows:
Your letter makes reference to a commitment made before the Parliamentary Committee by the former Executive Director of Immigration and Demographic Policy. In my view, we have completely conformed to that undertaking and have made the Immigration Manual available for use by the Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons on Statutory Regulations. We have, as well, instructed that these documents be made available for inspection at our offices throughout Canada to members of the public, and have deposited copies with the Library of Parliament. I do not view internal working memoranda of the type you have raised as falling into the category of documents that must be released to the public.
So, Mr. Speaker, we have given the hon. member all of the information he requires. I indicated that it was based on an
Privilege-Mr. Brewin
internal memorandum. I indicated that there was nothing else that needed to be disclosed.
We have tried to be open and above board with regard to this matter, because it is a matter of concern to many counsel who represent people who might be seeking refugee status in Canada. That information is certainly available to the public through the library and through our offices across Canada. If the hon. member feels that he has a case to put a motion for production of papers, we will debate that at that time, but I hardly think that his rights have been infringed upon.
Mir. Speaker: I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) rising. I want to tell him in advance that he will have to persuade me that this matter is distinct from any other application for a document from a minister resisted by the minister for his own reasons. In order to constitute this in any way as a question of privilege, there would have to be something which distinguishes it from an application for a document from the minister which the minister resists for his own reasons, whether I disagree or agree with
them.

maintopic: MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept your point as one that must be dealt with in supporting the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), but it seems to me there is a difference. First, the suggestion made by the minister that my friend should put his request in the form of a notice of motion for the production of papers would be futile since the minister has already said that he would refuse. There seems to be no possibility of getting anything by that method.
What makes this different from the ordinary document which a member tries to obtain through the order paper, it seems to me, is that in effect the clarifying memorandum is really an interpretation of the law. It is not good enough for a department to give to a citizen a statement of what is in the law or a precis of it. Citizens have a right to know what the law says, and that applies to acts which have been passed by parliament and to regulations passed under those acts.
What we have here is not a regulation passed under an act, but a departmental interpretation of the act and the regulations which in effect is the law covering the situation. It seems to me that on that basis the minister ought to be called upon to produce the document.
My hon. friend has suggested that he would be prepared to move a motion calling upon the minister to do so. If that suggestion is not acceptable, I have an alternative suggestion, that perhaps this matter ought to be referred to the committee on statutory instruments. If my case is valid, that it is in effect law, then I think that the document should be produced; but if that committee were to find that it was an internal document,
then,	of course, the minister's position would stand. Surely, the place for that kind of an issue to be settled is not in debate between the minister and the hon. member for Greenwood, but by some body which is competent to judge the nature of this document.

February 8, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Brewin

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to deal with this point. If he is indicating that this is added in some way to the body of law that every citizen is entitled to know and to receive, then how can I consider it to be a breach of privilege by a member of parliament? If it is something that is in that sense in the public domain and, as the hon. member maintains, it is a right which any citizen may assert, how can I classify it as the right only of a member of parliament in order to qualify it as a question of privilege? It seems to me that I am caught no matter in which direction I move.

maintopic: MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not suggesting that it is a privilege only of the hon. member for Greenwood or members of parliament. I am suggesting that the privileges of the citizens of this country are affected by the denial of this document to a member of parliament.
This matter is somewhat similar to the case raised by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) just recently. He had requested a document, not just for himself but for a constituent. My friend would like this document, which he believes is part of the law, so that all those named, the church organizations and individuals, will know what is in it. He does not want the document for himself but so that the public will know what is in it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
speechtext:
Either one or the other, Mr. Speaker. Either the directives given by the minister are part of the legislation in which case they are public and the hon. member may have access to them; or they are not part of the law and then it is up to the minister to communicate them to the hon. member or not. When the minister suggests a notice of motion for the production of papers which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) assumes will be rejected, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should know that this alternative would give the opportunity to launch a debate of over one hour in this House during which each member may get a chance to express his or her views instead of doing so by raising the question of privilege.
So to me, Mr. Speaker, the alternative is very clear, very simple: either these directives are part of the legislation and then they are public and it is not a question of privilege, as you did mention, or they have nothing to do with the piece of legislation itself and thus are not part of the law. In that case, the minister may or may not release them. There is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. BREWIN-REFUSAL OF MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION TO DIVULGE CONTENTS OF MEMORANDUM
speechtext:
Order. I repeat, I am not in a preliminary way persuaded that there is any difference from a regular application for a document held by a minister, but I think I owe it to the hon. members who have argued and urged the case that I research it. I will endeavour to do so as quickly as possible and

return with my ruling. I think I could give it by tomorrow, or at the very latest on Monday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wonder if 1 might ask the deputy government House leader, today being Thursday, if he could deal with the House business. Before he deals with the general business could he tell us whether or not he has had consultation with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) as to whether or not it is the intention of the Minister of Finance in this session of parliament to bring forward amendments to the Municipal Grants Act. I do not know how far we could go in dealing with the matter, but I have made the suggestion that a bill be brought forward containing the appropriate amendments and the subject matter be referred to a standing committee of the House. Once there it could be examined and municipal representatives from across the country could be called as witnesses. It is a problem that is not only common to the national capital but to other parts of Canada. If he has not had an opportunity to consult with the Minister of Finance with respect to that procedure, would he do so and advise the House today at some point?
While the minister is on his feet, could he tell us the government's intention with regard to legislative business on into next week?

Mr. Speaker, on the first point regarding amendments to the Municipal Grants Act, there is no doubt a great deal of concern about this across Canada, and to myself as well in my association with the Pickering airport expropriation issue. This subject is of great interest to the government, and we are giving consideration to the matter at the present time. I am not in a position to make a statement on behalf of the government as to the procedure which would be adopted to deal with that matter. I have not discussed it specifically in terms of a strategy here in the House with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), but I will undertake to do so and report back as soon as possible.
On the second point with regard to House business into next week, it is our intention, as all hon. members know, to continue today with Bill C-2. Following its completion, which should be very shortly today, we would then go to second reading of Bill C-12 which deals with the superannuation fund, and following that we will deal with Bill C-37, the amendments to the Income Tax Act and borrowing authority and Bill C-29, dealing with amendments to the National Housing Act. Then we would hope next week, if agreement can be reached between all parties, to deal with Bill C-35, which is the government organization bill. We would hope to reach agreement on limiting the debate to two or three speakers.
February 8, 1979

We also hope to deal next week with Bill C-28, the Northwest Territories Act legislation, if we can limit that debate to perhaps one speaker per party. In addition to that, tomorrow is an opposition day, and agreement has been reached for an allotted day for Tuesday, February 13.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly prepared to discuss with the deputy government House leader matters with respect to Bill C-35 and Bill C-28. I indicate to him that there is no intention to hold up that legislation. I will discuss this with him.
While I am on my feet, there is one other matter which is important. I thank the minister for his undertaking with respect to grants in lieu of taxes legislation. It is particularly important because, as the minister probably knows, the Minister of Finance is planning a meeting with the mayor of the city of Ottawa on February 19, and it would be interesting to know how he will be dealing with that legislation.
However, there is one other item which I do not know how to handle. I do not know whether I should address this matter to Your Honour as chairman of a committee which does not exist now, or whether I should address it to the deputy government House leader. I will take a chance and address it to the deputy government House leader. It has to do with the special committee which Your Honour chaired in the last session with respect to the broadcasting of the proceedings of the House of Commons. There was considerable discussion in that committee-and I must say that it was very amicable- with respect to the possibility of permitting the broadcasting, either through House of Commons facilities or through private broadcasting facilities, of the proceedings of the standing committees of the House of Commons. That is something we could perhaps deal with.
The unfortunate thing is that in this session there has not been a reference to re-establish that committee, which was working reasonably well. I think that if it is important that the general public look into the House of Commons to see what happens here, the public should recognize that this is only part of our work and that the daily grind of work in parliament and the process of legislation does not all take place here but that it also takes place in the standing committees. Even as this parliament is ending, I think it would be appropriate if that parliamentary committee were reconstituted. It might be able to do something, at the tail end of this parliament, relating to the broadcasting of committees. It might be able to do that, but it certainly could prepare for another parliament in any event, and I think that would be very helpful.
With respect to this parliament, I am sure that if we talked to representatives of the television media we would find that they would be anxious, on an ad hoc basis, to go into the committees.
There is a whole host of matters with which we have to deal, and if the deputy government House leader is not equipped today, would he speak to his colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), to see whether that reference
Business of the House
could be made so that that committee could be reconstituted under the chairmanship of Your Honour and we could get on with the work and finish it? If the minister cannot answer, would he give me an undertaking that he will at least speak to his colleague?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Quite evidently, the government is very much interested in making sure that the public has access to the deliberations of the House of Commons. It was for that reason that we introduced legislation to make that possible, so quite evidently the broad question raised by the hon. member about the reconstitution of the committee is important. Not having had notice of this question, I will indicate that I am prepared to take this matter up with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and my colleagues to find out what means might be best suited to the resolution of this question, and we will report back.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend for that. There is one matter with respect to Bill C-35 which I should like to raise. There have been some discussions about the possibility of splitting that bill so that the fisheries portion of it would go to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and the balance to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. We are willing to do that if that bill is to be brought forward and if that could be arranged.

Mr. Speaker, I have noted the various bills the minister has listed for debate for the next little while, and with respect to the two bills concerning which he thought there might need to be discussion, 1 would be quite prepared to enter into such discussions on behalf of my colleagues. However, since the point has now been raised here on the floor about the possibility of sending Bill C-35 in part to one committee and in part to another, we would go along with that. We think the House should take whatever steps are generally acceptable to proceed expeditiously with that bill.
While I am on my feet, I would like to ask the deputy government House leader if he, with all the urgency and concern he can command, will speak to his colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), and perhaps to other cabinet colleagues, about the desirability of bringing before this House, before something happens which might bring it to an end, at least some legislation respecting the veterans of this country.
There are three or four outstanding issues which are very serious. They should not be put over until the fall or to another year. Thus far there is nothing on the order paper. Nothing in sight is being done for Canadian veterans at this session, so I ask the deputy government House leader if he will raise this matter seriously and with concern with his colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the cooperative spirit which is being exhibited here today with respect to Bill C-35 and Bill C-28. In direct response to the

February 8, 1979
Point of Order-Mr. McKenzie
suggestion that Bill C-35 be split and sent in two directions to two different committees, I am not in a position to be able to respond in positive terms to that suggestion at the moment but we will deal with it. I understand the disposition of the Conservative party in that respect and the agreement of the House leader for the New Democratic Party. The second point raised is with respect to possible legislation dealing with veterans. Mr. Speaker, with respect to the confusion which is in the mind of the deputy government House leader, I am speaking with the consent of my House leader regarding the splitting of Bill C-35 to see to it that, as the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) wished, the fisheries part would go to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and the balance to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. We agree to that. I think my friends in the New Democratic Party would as well. 1 do not know whether they have had any consultation in this regard, but I think that is the general feeling at this time, and I am sure-
That is what 1 said. We agree.

Perhaps I was being overly cautious. It is my understanding that that is likely to be the case, but I do not like to stand here before the House and make an absolute commitment that that will happen without having certainty in my mind. maintopic: MR. McKINNON-BOEING CONTRACT-EVIDENCE GIVEN BEFORE SEC
MR. McKINNON-BOEING CONTRACT-EVIDENCE GIVEN BEFORE SEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) for remaining in the chamber to hear my point of order. My point of order concerns an answer he gave to me during the question period. 1 raised a question based on a detailed answer he had given to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) on February 6 concerning the Boeing agent and his activities. There is quite a bit of information in that answer which is not readily available.
The Solicitor General in his answer said:
The individual who testified before the SEC-
-and I presumed he had the testimony that was given before the SEC. Today the Solicitor General claimed that it was
February 8, 1979

obtained from a deposition given on behalf of the Boeing company in front of the SEC. That deposition came as a result of a civil action commenced by the Securities and Exchange Commission dated July 1978 against Boeing. The action was heard by the district court, and a judgment was given concerning this matter. In the judgment Boeing had to comply with several conditions. Among these conditions was a requirement to file form 8-K with the commission. In accepting these conditions Boeing agreed to disclose information in a current report on form 8-K for the month of July 1978. The document goes on to require "Any instances of the existence of two consulting contracts with the same consultant providing for payments of compensation under each contract for the same services designed to facilitate the payment of money into accounts maintained by the consultant outside his own country". This was duly filed on July 28, 1978. I have the document here and it is some 15 pages long. Nowhere in that deposition or indeed in any of the other documents I have quoted from is there any word about who the individual is. And yet the Solicitor General gave us to understand on Tuesday that he knew. Because the Leader of the Opposition asked the minister:
-does he know the name or names of the person or persons alleged to have received those payments mentioned in the deposition from Boeing-
The Solicitor General answered:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The individual who testified before the SEC was a gentleman who was identified as a consultant of Boeing and who was working as a Boeing consultant in Canada dealing with the sale of Boeing aircraft to Canada. Payments were made to that consultant in the ordinary course of dealing with that company.
There is not one word of this in the deposition. It says that double payments were made in Canada to obtain the Canadian sales. I do not know, and the House does not know, where the Solicitor General obtained this detailed information about the agent. One would assume that he probably obtained it because the agent testified before a subcommittee of the SEC on March 24, 1977, some nine days after that sweetheart treaty was signed between the two governments protecting anyone who gave evidence which was likely to be disadvantageous to either government. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to resume my comments on Bill C-2, to amend the Health Resources Fund Act to remove $84 million over a period of two years from medical funding programs in Canada. This bill

February 8, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
reflects the callousness and irresponsibility of this government, not to mention its lamentable management ability.
When my time expired yesterday, I was recounting a few of the landmarks in medical research that had been achieved in Canada. I pointed out that the cost of a medical research breakthrough is negligible in terms of the benefits derived from such discoveries. I mentioned the discovery of insulin and polio vaccine in this context.
The potential for further discoveries of this magnitude exists right now here in Canada. In my constituency of St. Boniface, heart research of an internationally recognized high level is being conducted at the St. Boniface General Hospital. This group receives thousands of dollars from the public through the St. Boniface Research Foundation. Its work has been recognized by some of the most prestigious medical pioneers in the world. Dr. Jonas Salk, who developed the polio vaccine and Dr. Christian Barnard, the heart transplant genius, have both visited and spoken on behalf of the St. Boniface Research Foundation in an effort to raise funds for the prolongation of heart research at that institution. Just last year the Duke of Edinburgh spoke on behalf of research at that institution.
The same is true of the biomedical engineering program in that the dollar efficiency of funds invested in this area is very high. My colleague from Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) in a previous presentation cited a comment by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) when he was minister of national health and welfare to the effect that the handicapped must be given the opportunity to participate fully in our society. This goal, and it is a very worth-while one, can only be realized through advances in biomedical engineering.
Some three quarters of the health resources fund was earmarked for construction of facilities for training health professionals and acquiring research equipment. This latter specification would indicate that the cuts announced will affect support for biomedical engineering research. What has happened to the government's pledge of 1973 to help the handicapped become independent of institutions which had never been more than palliatives for their problems? Let me quote from a report in today's Globe and Mail in which doctors at several teaching hospitals are quoted. The article states:
Tight budgeting by Ontario's health ministry has left teaching hospitals hurting most and complaining loudest about their inability to keep pace with advances in medical science. Recent interviews with senior staffs at four teaching hospitals and two community hospitals in Toronto, Timmins, Ottawa and London have revealed that an absence of money for new programs and equipment is at the top of a list of concerns arising out of the budget squeeze.
Further, Dr. Wilbert Keon, chief of surgery at the Ottawa Civic Hospital, is quoted as saying:
Academically, doctors see no new horizons ... Many new methods and techniques are happening in the medical field that you would like to apply but no way here. It gets discouraging.
And so on. These reports show that the statements originally made by the minister when presenting this bill that medical research and medical funding are up to requirements are not accurate. They demonstrate that experts in the medical field

are already being hurt by budgetary constraints, that their work is being hamstrung and that they are falling behind. Now the federal government is proposing further cuts which will be heaped on top of the provincial health cuts.
Canada possesses expertise in health research, especially in biomedical engineering. Our interest in the subject is borne out by the fact that in 1980 the city of Winnipeg is hosting the Rehabilitation International Congress to which some 6,000 handicapped persons will attend. I submit that our expertise in biomedical engineering as it bears upon rehabilitation will not be fully exploited if legislation such as Bill C-2 is allowed to pass. How can we be sincere in conducting a conference on rehabilitation when our own efforts in the field are so constrained?
I should like to speak for a while on research efforts with which I myself am particularly familiar. In my own research field of nutritional biochemistry I was privileged to have been involved in some of the earlier work leading to the discovery of vitamin B-12, originally known as the unidentified growth factor. It has been shown that in the absence of this vitamin a condition of pernicious anemia cannot be overcome. In other facets of biochemistry and nutrition it has been shown that microfactors are important in the health control of individuals. Consider the position of a patient in hospital who has a particular deficiency. How would hon. members feel if it were shown that, because of lack of equipment or because a research finding was not available, that patient suffered severely? In many cases the result is the death of the patient. When are members on the opposite side going to get themselves out from under the yoke of this present flip-flop direction under a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who arbitrarily alters his horses in the middle of the stream? Possibly, the answer to my question will only be given by the people at the next election.

To judge from the debate so far, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's remarks are in keeping with those made by his hon. friends on the other side-absolutely foolish and totally uncalled for. When the health services fund was established in 1966 there were 12 schools of medicine and 800 doctors graduating. What has happened since then? We are now graduating 1,700 doctors per year. We have spent considerable amounts of money upgrading medical schools and increasing their numbers. We have at the present time the capacity to accommodate 2,500 doctors in classes in the universities and similar establishments, but 1,700 are actually in place.
Health Resources Fund Act
The opposition is saying that what we should be doing is spending millions of dollars to put up more buildings and provide more equipment in order to graduate more doctors. The situation is such in the medical profession, for example, that we could graduate an additional 800 because we have space for them. What the opposition is saying is that we should not see how many people we have there, let us just spend the money. The fact that we have now produced the plants and the facilities for doctors that are in keeping with the demand apparently has no meaning to the opposition. They say that regardless whether we have full plants in operation to meet Canadian needs, what we should do is to continue spending money on the expansion of these facilities. 1 find that very hard to accept from a party which claims it is looking for ways to cut down government expenditure, the same party which now says that regardless whether we have fulfilled our obligations, which we did, we should continue with that program even though the facilities are not needed.
It is a fact that the total number of dentists who graduated in 1977 was 350. That number has increased dramatically to the point that we are one of the best served nations so far as dentists go.
With regard to nurses, 7,000 graduated in 1966, and now 10,000 have graduated. The fact that we have probably no more jobs available for nurses due to the fact that we have one of the highest nurse-patient ratios apparently has escaped the hon. member who rose on a point of order. His proposal is, I suppose, that we should continue expanding nursing schools even though we do not need more nurses.
I point this out only because we are not proposing to cut down on essential services to people. Quite the contrary, the Liberal government established in 1966 a significant program to assist the provinces in providing facilities for doctors, dentists, nurses and dental assistants. The Conservative party and others say that regardless whether or not we achieve that, we should keep spending money to increase it. I say to hon. members that if they wish to debate the particular point of the necessity for added facilities for training doctors, nurses and dentists, then they should come up with statistics to show it.
I ask the hon. member who spoke before me this. I wonder what provinces have come forward since a telex advising the provinces of this program was sent out in September demanding that the federal government continue the expansion of teaching facilities. The silence is deafening. However, apparently this does not stop the opposition parties which say that we should still go on with the program.
I intervened for a few minutes for one reason only. Since we are dealing with an equipment and construction program which has served the people of Canada well, is it not foolish to continue with a program which is not necessary at this time? It might be necessary at some time in the future; additonal facilities might be required at some time. However, at this time when we as a government are attempting to be responsible in assessing where money is most needed, that particular area is not one with a high priority.

Mr. Speaker, if we can skip the last speaker, I should like to say how pleased I am to have the opportunity to follow the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Hare). In relation to the last speaker I should like to express my absolute and total surprise that someone would come to this House and make a submission that we have already spent all the money to give us the adequate number of doctors and dentists, and that we have a full complement of nurses, no more being needed. Certainly he must be a person who has not visited a senior citizens' home or a nursing home in recent years or he has not been around medical institutions recently. Because if he had, he would have recognized that what he said is a blatant misunderstanding of the facts of Canadian life. I might say that what he misunderstands are the facts of Canadian ill health in terms of the situation we would have, the need for nursing homes and the like.
He said that we had some of the Finest medical facilities but that all this party wanted to do was to spend money. The truth is that it is not a question whether or not the federal government is spending money; it is a question whether or not the federal government is getting out of a commitment. This government has a commitment with the provinces of this country which it should live up to.
While the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) stands in his place and states that the government has no need to fulfil that commitment, that it spends money wisely-as is shown by Mirabel airport no doubt-I submit that it is not by chance that not one of the medical doctors on the government side of the House has chosen to speak on this bill. I think it should be pointed out that there are three medical doctors on the other side of the House. There is a doctor from the constituency of Halton (Mr. Philbrook), a doctor from the constituency of Hull (Mr. Isabelle) and a doctor from the constituency of Welland (Mr. Railton). Not one of them chose to speak. It will be interesting to see whether or not they are in the House when the time comes to vote.
What is more important, they have to ask themselves the serious question whether they will vote yes to restrict medical services in this country, being as they are in the profession of medicine. Because we have before us a bill to cut the contract by $84 million. The new title for the minister should now be the "minister of wealth and hellfare". Hers has been a Robin Hood attack upon the poor, leaving the rich to fend for themselves because, in her view now, they are the only ones who can.
This bill breaches humanitarian purposes. It is a bill which reflects bad faith in negotiations and contracts with the provinces. It restricts health services and facilities, and it has callous disregard for the health needs of this country.
The position of the government party has been that they are doing this out of a concept of restraint. Since we on this side have been a party which has always favoured restraint, the government party tends to say that there is a conflict therein. The problem is that there is only one taxpayer, whether he pays municipal, provincial or federal taxes. When services are needed, the options are simply these: either the federal govern-

ment will pay for them or the provincial government will have to pick up the tab. If the provincial government does not, then the citizen at large will have to pay. The funds come from the same source anyway. If the citizen at large does not pick up the tab, you will have the simple and obvious result of inadequate health services.
I submit that what we have here in this bill is not a question whether we are saving or losing money, but whether or not we have a government that is in breach of contract. This is a government which has promised the provinces it will fund until 1981 a program which has some $84 million yet to be spent. The government is saying that it will now cut off that program without giving notice.
The fact that the government did not give notice caused some considerable damage. I should like to refer to some of the damage which has occurred across the country. Now the Government of Canada is faced with a more expensive situation than it would have faced if it managed to keep the program going. For example, at the time the program was cancelled, a druggist in Alberta had 14 prescriptions for native and Indian people, 13 of which were for children under the age of six. Because the program was cancelled, those people were unable to get their prescriptions filled. On the average the prescriptions cost $12, but because they are unable to get the prescriptions filled, their choice is a day in hospital costing $120. If the government assumes that this cutback will save money, it is just another example of not knowing the facts of the situation. Only two days' notice was given to the druggist that the plan would be abandoned, and the native people received no notice whatsoever. That is an example of harsh and callous treatment by a department in the medical health services field. Its principal objective ought to be a humanitarian one.
I could not agree more with the article which appeared in the Toronto Star on April 13, 1978 at page 10. It is entitled: "Research support 'scandalous' ". It fully documents that Canadian research is scandalous. Also I agree with the article entitled: "Boss Begin's in trouble" which appeared in the January 27, 1979 edition of the Toronto Star. It attacked the administration of the Department of National Health and Welfare, now renamed the "department of wealth and hell-fare". In part that article reads:
-but disdain for her inab lity to provide direction and fiscal control.
It continued:
-her department is floundering under her scattergun approach and her indecisive dodging.
Further on it reads:
But they all suggest it is not easy working with a minister who is so nervous that she has specifically ordered senior officials not to discuss her, who is suspicious of all those who hold opposing points of view, who often blames others for her errors and whose tremendous personal warmth and intelligence is marred by bursts of impatience and erratic concentration.

Returning to the article dealing with Canada's position on research, it reads:
"No other nation of the western world has treated biomedical research in such a disastrous way"-
The author of the article is referring to Canada. It continues:
-the budget of the Medical Research Council of Canada declined from .38 of the gross national product in 1967 to .26 per cent in 1976.
There is a continuing decrease in our research budget. It continues:
In the same period, the percentage spent on biomedical research of the total spent on health care in Canada went down from 1.12 in 1969 to .46 in 1976-
In other words, it was not cut to half, it was cut to approximately a third in less than a decade. The article continues:
"One of the results of this policy was that between 300 and 400 biomedical research workers were lost in the fierce competition for funds"-
Earlier the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) said that we have plenty of people, but interestingly enough he was not aware of Canadian medical needs. The hon. member is quite content to submit to an adequate situation when researchers are chased out of the country because of the $84 million cutback.
It is interesting to note that only a few Liberal members have spoken in favour of this piece of legislation, yet not one medical doctor on their side has risen. Also it will be interesting to see what the hon. member for Halton, the hon. member for Hull and the hon. member for Welland will do when the vote on this particular bill takes place.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) stated that the half-life of a physician's knowledge is somewhere between five and seven years. 1 would like to add that the half-life of a government minister is about six months, and it is just that-a half-life. This government though seldom awake is now celebrating one. In 1976 the federal government gave its word to the provinces through the health resources fund that there would be adequate health facilities, adequate funding for personnel and research and for the provision of a necessary health delivery system. With that commitment the provinces set out their programs.

February 8, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
I am sure we all know that there comes a time when you back off if the situation warrants it and you have mutual agreement. The fact of the matter is that the provinces were not consulted here. It is interesting to go through the data, province by province from the Pacific to the Atlantic, because therein you will find that virtually not a single province was consulted by this government on its decision to withdraw the remaining funds under this program. Sure, they received phone calls from someone who said: Hey, guess what; we are cutting the program. There was no consultation about a phaseout, or advance notice of the suggestion that this government was going to cut this program off at some future date, with a date specified.
What in fact has happened is that the provinces from sea to sea have made plans one or two years ahead for the construction of facilities. They have hired architects and put staffs into position on the basis of a commitment by the federal government in respect of ongoing funds through to 1981. The government now is simply slicing off $84 million with the net result that, while there has been consultation to the extent of phone calls, the provinces are left in the disastrous situation of having to curtail programs for which they have already committed the funds. What we have in essence is a game in respect of which the rules have been changed in mid-play.
This government has dealt a raw, rough and callous blow to the provinces of this country. The situation could have been different had things occurred as suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and that is with consultation with the provinces and agreement to cut the program back. That would have been a very different situation. However, to allow these provinces to go ahead and commit funds-I will document that in a few minutes-and then cut off the money without consultation, leaving provinces such as Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and the rest carrying the burden of the cost of projects to which they have committed themselves, can in no way be considered a savings for the taxpayers of this country.
The federal government has chintzied out of its obligations by saying it is saving money, only to force the taxpayers to fund these projects from another pocket because of provincial commitments. That is not fair, and certainly it is not fair government. It is about time this kind of tactic of pretending the government is cutting back, when all it is doing is shifting the burden of expense, should be made clear to Canadians from coast to coast, so that at the time of the next election they will know that if they put this government back they will have unfair government.
What this government has done is cut down on the number of dollars available for health care. As a result of this cutback the people have been given a choice. The burden must now be shifted to the provinces, municipalities or to family budgets, or, in the alternative, the public must put up with inadequate health and, in the final analysis, death itself. That is really what will be the result of this government's cutting down on funds available.
Since we are debating a bill relating to health, I should like to say it is very unfortunate that in the consideration of health care we have adopted programs that have been intact for years and essentially look after the health of Canadians from the epiglotis down. In other words, they look after you from your epiglotis to your toenails, but they are unconcerned with the human head. Our health programs do not look after the teeth or the eyes, will not provide a hearing aid if that is what an individual needs, and do not take care of psychiatric expenses. Under the Canadian concept one can have a perfectly healthy body but health programs do not cover the head.
It seems to me this has derived from some medieval thinking that if for some reason an individual is insane he should be put in a basket and spun about because this condition is not covered by health care. If this government thinks that is some reason for cutting back, perhaps it is time we started providing medical care from the larynx up, or started looking after the whole human being including teeth, eyes, ears and psychiatric needs where there is evident necessity.
I have often condemned this government for its failure to consult with the provinces. Let me refer to what some of the provincial ministers of health have stated in relation to the question whether there was consultation on the part of this government before it decided to cut $84 million from provincial services. According to Mr. Collins, minister of health for Newfoundland, he was informed only and not consulted. He said he was quite unhappy about Bill C-2 because Newfoundland has no more money now to help out with the health services centre at the university in St. John's. That is very unfortunate because this is money which the province has already committed. That will now become a burden on the taxpayers of that province.

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
Hon. members will recall that on December 12, 1978,1 gave an undertaking to the House that the government would not attempt to alter public service pensions indexing arrangements in a retroactive manner. To give effect to this undertaking I will be proposing a number of amendments to the bill at an appropriate stage in the consideration of it. Virtually all of these amendments will concern themselves with effective dates: an effective date of January 1, 1980, for the introduction of the triennial pension supplementation arrangements described in the bill so that the first review and decision on these arrangements would apply to the 1980-82 period; an effective date of April 1, 1979, for implementation of the proposals respecting the deferral and prorating of pension supplementation payments and the commencement of the collection of extra current service employee contributions required by air traffic controllers for the improvement in their pension benefits which is proposed in the bill; and that all

other proposals come into effect upon Royal Assent of the bill. Finally, I should like to mention that the delay in parliament's consideration of the bill has given the government an opportunity to carry out a general review of the bill. Accordingly, a few amendments will be introduced to clarify and improve several areas of the bill. I should add that none of the proposed amendments in this category involve pension benefits provisions.
Now I should like to turn to the objectives of the bill which I listed at the outset of my remarks. The most important one by far, in terms of principle and the number of people it affects, is the one concerned with modifying the arrangement under which the pensions of former public servants, military and RCMP personnel, and members of parliament now are automatically indexed with changes in the consumer price index. Bill C-12 proposes that the existing arrangement be changed in two fundamental respects. It proposes the removal of the automatic feature which now exists, and the removal of the continuing requirement that the adjustments be calculated in accordance with the consumer price index.
In my view these changes will go a long way toward resolving the central controversies in the public service pension debate. I think I speak for most members of the House when I say that resolution of the key public service pensions issues has been hampered seriously by some of the emotional and distorted arguments inflicted upon Canadians over the past few years on the costs and economic consequences associated with treating pensioners in a fair and humane manner.

I regret to say we have not seen the end of these emotional distortions. Indeed, we have just witnessed another one of the National Citizens' Coalition periodic newspaper ad diatribes on the subject. This latest outburst of the coalition indicates that the government has received a new report on public service pensions. The ad suggests attempts have been made to suppress the report which the coalition describes as a "shocker", because, in its view, it demonstrates public service pensions are costing or will cost taxpayers an extra $5,160 annually for each public servant, in short, an extra annual cost of over $1.5 billion, for a total over-all cost of $2 billion. What a pile of rubbish!
Let me outline briefly the facts of the situation. The report mentioned is not a new one. It was submitted to the govern-

ment in December, 1977, and released to the public on March 9, 1978. The suggestion that the report was suppressed is ridiculous. Copies of the report were circulated to all members of the House, the Press Gallery, unions, business firms, interested associations, and many libraries across Canada. Even today, more than a year after its completion, the report is being sent to individual Canadians upon request.
The statement that public service pensions will cost taxpayers $2 billion annually is sheer nonsense. In this regard I merely point out the employer contributions underwritten last year by taxpayers for both basic public service pensions and their indexing amounted to $490 million. That works out to 10.8 per cent of payroll, not 34.4 per cent. Furthermore, if Bill C-12 were enacted, it will ensure that over-all employer contributions for public service pensions will be restricted to 10 per cent to 12 per cent of payroll, the average level wich prevailed during the 1950s and 1960s before public service pensions were indexed. In terms of its impact on taxpayers, in short, Bill C-12 turns the public service pension clock back to the same stage as they were in the 1950s and 1960s,
It is important to recognize the latest coalition ad for what it really is: a mathematically orchestrated exercise, replete with partial truths and innuendoes, to persuade Canadians to fight inflation on the backs of pensioners, widows and the disabled. This is a most odious and reprehensible form of discrimination because clearly pensioners, widows and the disabled, are the victims and not the cause of inflation. I am confident Canadians will reject the call to fight inflation by victimizing the victims of inflation. Indeed, I should like to take this occasion publicly to urge the coalition to use its considerable energy and resources to join other Canadians in working toward a fair and humane deal for all pensioners, widows and disabled Canadians.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The most serious consequence of the highly publicized campaign conducted against the indexing of pensions has been its effect in polarizing extremist opinion on the subject. This polarization has had the unfortunate result of distracting public attention from the more thoughtful and quietly expressed opinions of those with a genuine concern for both the welfare of pensioners and the Canadian economy. Those who have taken this balanced approach in the indexing debate have been correct in drawing attention to the fact inflation brings about increases, not only in the consumer price index but also in interest rates. This simple fact means that properly managed employer pension plans have a considerable built-in financial capacity to repair the damage inflation creates in the incomes of pensioners.
The fact inflation has an effect on both the costs and revenues of an employer pension plan effectively exposes the Achilles heel in the position of the indexing doomsayers. Nevertheless, it must be recognized that while extra earnings realized by properly managed employer pension plans, in times of inflation, go a long way to answering the concerns about indexing costs, they do not answer these concerns completely.
February 8, 1979

It must be stressed that inflationary pension fund earnings are capable only of meeting inflationary pension costs entirely if interest rates and other investment returns keep in step with the consumer price index. If inflationary earnings cannot keep up with inflationary costs, and if employer and employee pension contributions ear-marked for indexing are insufficient to close the gap, the inevitable result is a deficit which usually must be financed by employers. And when the employer pension plans are operated by government, the financing of these deficits falls upon the taxpayer.
The underlying thrust of Bill C-12, hon. members will recognize, is directed at meeting this concern by ensuring that the extra earnings of the pension program are sufficient to meet supplemention costs. To achieve this objective, the bill proposes to convert the pension adjustment features of the program into a money purchase approach along the lines that were described in the House on March 9, 1978. In other words, the bill proposes that public service employee pensions, in future, be adjusted according to the degree of supplementation that can generally be financed or purchased by the funds becoming available from extra interest earned on pensioner money in the program, and the special employer and employee contributions that have been made for indexing. The bottom line result of this approach is that it will provide taxpayers with a statutory assurance that the government employer contributions required of them to finance these supplements will be reduced and restricted to the order of 1 per cent of payroll. This, in my view, will place the program on a more financially responsible and equitable basis from the points of view of both those who will be receiving the supplements and those who will be paying for them.
Since the intentions of the government to adopt this new principle in public service pension arrangements were announced, there has been an encouraging show of support for this proposed concept. In this regard, I take particular satisfaction out of the degree of all-party support that was demonstrated in the House when the concept was first described here in March of last year. In addition, shortly thereafter, I was pleased to learn that the approach that was being proposed for the federal public service was similar to an approach being advocated for the private sector by the Cofirentes Plus Committee of business and government officials which has been examining public and private pension arrangements in the province of Quebec for the last few years. According to the April 8, 1978, edition of the Financial Post, the Cofirentes Plus Committee concluded that the dilemma of uncertainty that indexing creates for employers and that its absence creates for pensioners might be resolved by the introduction of legislation, and, I quote:
-to require at least partial indexing of private pension plans to the cost-of-living. The committee recommends that excess interest over the assumed actuarial rate on funds invested for pensioners should be used to improve pensions.
The approach also appears to have struck a responsive chord amongst some sections of the actuarial community judging
Pensions
from a statement that a prominent Canadian actuary made before a group of actuaries last summer when he said:
-it is now the perceived, conventional wisdom among private employers that only governments can afford it (indexing). The facts, I think, are rather different. Of course, indexing, especially open-ended unlimited indexing for the full increase in the consumer price index, is expensive, and the cost is not only significant but highly volatile because the incidence of inflation itself is so volatile. However, the cost is finite, not infinite, and the volatility can be controlled through appropriate limitations on full indexing and through a commitment to devote the inflationary element of investment income on pensioner liabilities to meeting whatever the costs may be.
That cheer from the lobby obviously means that the Canadians have scored a goal in the Russian-NHL Challenge Cup game. I can tell that I am running tough competition tonight.

As I mentioned a few moments ago, Bill C-12 effectively puts public service pension supplementation arrangements on a money purchase basis, and so deals head-on with the issue of cost uncertainty that is generally associated with indexing arrangements. Consequently, if Bill C-12 is enacted, I think we will see a change occurring in the key question that is usually asked about the indexing of public service pensions; that is, with the enactment of C-12, the question "How much will indexing cost?" should gradually give way to the question "How much indexing will there be?" Indeed, like other members of the House, I am finding that this change is already taking place in the correspondence I am receiving on the subject.
Given the prospect that pension supplements would have to be curtailed if earmarked revenues are insufficient for full indexing, I feel it is important that other features of the program be re-examined so that we can assure ourselves that the supplementation arrangements, taken as a whole, are fair and equitable in terms of their over-all impact on different groups of pensioners. When such an examination is carried out, I think it must be concluded that some features of the program are not as fair as they could be.
One feature of the program that is widely regarded as being unfair is the provision which gives public servants retiring at the end of the year the same post-retirement adjustment as those retiring at the beginning of the year. No reasonable person, I believe, could take issue with the statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on March 9, 1978, when he said:
This idea that a person can retire on December 29 or 30 on full pension, and then get a year's indexation two or three days later, just does not wash.
Bill C-12 proposes to correct this situation by prorating the first adjustment granted to new pensioners according to the length of their retirement in the first calendar year. With the amendment I will be proposing, new pensioners will in effect mean individuals becoming eligible for pension benefits on and after April 1, 1978.

The savings resulting from this change will obviously make more money available for the supplements of other pensioners.
Another feature of the program that requires re-examination is the provision which, in some instances, allows individuals receiving pensions before the age of 60 to receive immediate indexing payments. Generally speaking, individuals drawing pensions before the age of 60, because of their younger age at retirement, will receive pension payments for a longer period than those retiring at age 60 or later. In these circumstances, we must ask ourselves if it is fair that those who draw basic pensions for the longest periods of time should, on top of this advantage, also be allowed to collect pension adjustments for a longer period than those who retire at age 60 or later. In other words, is it fair that "those who have, get, and those who don't, don't?" Bill C-12 deals with this situation by proposing the general deferment of pension supplement payments to age 60.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: It depends on how long they live.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
That is true, but actuarially they should all live the same average number of years.
Fairness, however, dictates that some exceptions be made to this change, and that the change itself be implemented in a fair manner. Accordingly, Bill C-12 proposes that payment of pension supplements not be deferred for individuals who have already retired; nor for current and future recipients of disability pensions or survivor benefits. The bill, with the proposed amendment 1 have described, also provides that the change be implemented gradually so that for those who leave the public service this year, on and after April 1, 1979, 56 would be the earliest age at which the supplements could be collected; for those who leave the public service in 1980, the earliest qualifying age for receiving the supplementation payments would be 57; for those who leave in 1981, the minimum qualifying age for receiving pension supplements would be age 58, and so on. The savings resulting from this change, like those resulting from the prorating change, would have the general effect of minimizing any curtailment that may be required in the triennial supplementation arrangements, particularly after 1982 when the change would be fully operative.
I want to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to say that the principle of fairness among pensioners is the principle that the government also intends to follow whenever the three-year reviews, which are required under the bill, produce forecasts of revenues from extra pensioner interest earnings and indexing contributions as defined in the bill that will be insufficient to finance fully indexed supplements. The bill provides that when such situations arise pension supplements must be curtailed to match income revenues. The simplest way of doing this, of course, would be on an across-the-board basis, that is, for

example, by authorizing supplements equal to 90 per cent of the expected increase in the consumer price index if that is what triennial forecasts indicate is all we can afford. Although simple and easily understood, such an approach, in my opinion, would not be an equitable one for those on the lower end of the pension income scale.
As we all know, pensioners with low incomes have a particularly difficult time in coping with a reduction in the purchasing value of their incomes. Consequently, when revenue shortfalls require a curtailment of pension supplements, the arrangements established cannot, in my view, be determined solely on a cold balance-sheet basis. In short, I believe that fairness and equity require a measure of full indexing up to some minimum benefit level.
The periodic establishment and review of an appropriate benefit level for full indexing must, of course, begin with a realistic assessment of the amount of money that will become available from the earmarked sources defined in the bill. Once this assessment is made, some account must also be taken of the fact that employer pension plans are not designed and looked upon, primarily, as instruments for redistributing income among individuals. Many Canadians, I think, regard employer pension and savings plans as being generally similar in their objectives, and so consider that the benefits provided by employer pension plans should bear a recognizable relationship to the contributions, financial and otherwise, that individuals make to these plans and their sponsoring employers.
This notion of pensions being a return on the contributory savings of employees and pensioners is, of course, being reinforced by Bill C-12. In summary, I feel that the triennial supplementation arrangements that are authorized for public service pensioners must reflect a humane understanding of the situation faced by low income pensioners. At the same time, I think it must be recognized that there are limits on the degree to which supplementation payments can be divorced from the pension savings of individuals, and the earnings realized on their pensions savings or contributions.
I presented to the House earlier this month the proposed supplementation arrangements that would have been put in place if, in fact, this particular bill had received royal proclamation prior to the end of last year. Hon. members will recall that $7,000 would have been the proposed point for division. There would be full indexation up to earnings of $7,000, and above that the figure proposed was 8 per cent in 1979, 7 per cent in 1980, and 6 per cent in 1981.
