chief actuary in the latter part of this year. The thought is that we may be able to move it up from $7,000 to $7,500 or perhaps $8,000. However, we will not be able to determine that until later this year.
Bill C-12 indirectly also requires that the triennial reviews and establishment of pension supplementation arrangements be carried with an eye to the future. This need arises from the requirement that any surplus or deficit realized with respect to any three-year period must be carried forward to the next three-year period. Consequently, triennial arrangements that are overly optimistic in one period could produce relatively restrictive arrangements and disappointment for pensioners in the future periods because the bottom line provision of Bill C-12 is that pensioners, not taxpayers, must meet any pension supplementation deficits.

speechtext: What about the reverse?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asks what about the reverse. There could not be a reverse. This fund is earmarked for pensioners. In other words, is the hon. member asking if we would go above full cost?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: Suppose that the calculations were too pessimistic.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I don't think that would happen. It might be that one could change the arrangement in mid-stream, but the fund is earmarked and is, in effect, the property of retired pensioners. If they did not receive as much in one period, then they would receive a larger amount in succeeding periods. It is their fund, in the sense that it is earmarked for this special purpose. It is clearly identifiable and, therefore, if there is an inadequate amount paid out in one period, then we would have the option to make changes during that period or, certainly, the funds which had not been dispersed would remain in the fund and be available for future supplementation.
In practical terms, this means that to achieve fairness in treatment between current and future pensioners, it will be necessary that three-year reviews of supplementation revenues and benefits avoid optimistic and pessimistic extremes.
Taking all these factors into account, I am confident that when the review is carried out in the second half of this year of the revenues that will become available over the next three years from the pensioners' share of extra interest earnings and the special contributions that have been made by and for pensioners to the indexing account, it will be possible to establish an arrangement whereby the first $7,000 of annual public service pension, disability and survivor benefits, could be fully indexed in 1980, 1981 and 1982. If this were done, it would mean that over 95 per cent of recipients of disability and survivor benefits would have their pensions fully indexed. In addition, I am confident that the supplementation revenue picture will be such that it will still be possible to provide higher income pensioners with a reasonable return on their contributions to the program.
Pensions
Much of my confidence in this regard, Mr. Speaker, is based on the healthy growth in interest earnings being achieved by the public service pension accounts, and the clear evidence that this growth will continue into the foreseeable future. Also it is based on the forecasts being made by reputable financial institutions for a moderation in inflationary pressures over the coming year. We believe that the meld of these two factors should allow us, as I mentioned a moment ago, to present a more attractive picture at the end of this year for the following three-year period. The actual amounts of supplementation authorized for 1980 to 1982 cannot, of course, be determined until the forecasts of revenues available for the supplements are received this fall from the government actuary.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the remaining portions of the bill. These portions of the bill directly affect less than 1 per cent of public servants, with the vast majority of them being air traffic controllers. The proposals contained in the bill to establish special pension provisions for air traffic controllers are designed to ensure the continued maintenance of high safety standards for air travel in Canada, and to provide income protection for air traffic controllers who may be detrimentally affected by the application of these standards.
These provisions are the product of an agreement which was reached with the air traffic controllers' union in 1976 to deal with the situation of air traffic controllers who failed the rigid examinations they must regularly take to retain their licences as air traffic controllers. The program agreed to with the controllers encompasses the provision of special training to prepare controllers for other work, the partial drawing down of pension benefits and, as a last resort, the payment of early retirement pensions earned by air traffic controllers who are compulsorily retired after a minimum of ten years' service in an air traffic control tower. In addition, the bill would allow air traffic controllers to draw unreduced pensions upon voluntary early retirement if they are at least 50 years of age and have a minimum of 25 years' service in an aircraft control tower.
I want to stress that all of the service requirements for these special pension provisions for air traffic controllers involve service in an air traffic control tower. In other words, if a 50 year old air traffic controller had 27 years of service in the public service but only 20 years' service in an air traffic control tower, he would not qualify for an immediate unreduced pension upon voluntary retirement. I also want to add that in return for these special pension features, air traffic controllers will be required to make an extra 2 per cent pension contribution, and this extra contribution will be matched by the government as employer.
The bill also contains a provision which would allow the government to follow the private sector practice of amortizing unfunded actuarial liabilities over a 15-year period instead of over a five-year period in the event the chief actuary should alter his economic assumptions or the actuarial method by

February 8, 1979
Pensions
which he carries out his evaluations of public service superannuation accounts.
The remaining provisions of the bill are directed at overcoming administrative difficulties and correcting benefit anomalies in various pension statutes which in total involve less than 50 individuals.
1 would like to conclude by reminding hon. members, as my predecessor did on March 9 of last year, that the introduction of this bill does not represent a finalization of the government's review of public service pension arrangements. The scrutiny of these arrangements will continue, with future analyses and decisions taking account of the actuarial valuation of the program which is now being carried out by the department of insurance, the total compensation analyses which are being carried out by the Treasury Board secretariat, and the results of the government's review of the retirement income situation facing all Canadians.

There is confusion. I would like to quote from a recent postscript in the Ottawa Journal of February 7, 1979. words the minister used. He says there will be a humane approach and that after study and if possible, the limit for people in the $7,000 bracket will be raised to $7,500 or even $8,000. For example, in his January report to voters Liberal MP Lloyd Francis tells his constituents: "There is a serious question about the fund itself being over-funded and within a very short time the Government of Canada is going to be embarrassed by the amount of money in the fund.''
Francis says there is more than $9 billion in the superannuation account at the moment. Well, we have not received the answer from the President of the Treasury Board. The Auditor General has been involved with a threepronged thrust; as he puts it, the economy, efficiency, and effectiveness. He is including as well value for money, waste, and management. It seems to me that the President of the Treasury Board has accepted the thrust of the Auditor General and accordingly has now picked-and I have another word that 1 will use later-on the public service. What was the scenario as far as members of this House and public servants were concerned? There was a scenario prior to the speculation of the last election. Do you recall when the code of ethics was brought in
February 8, 1979

Mr. Speaker? Canadians were concerned about how public servants act. The vast majority are doing a tremendous job, at some sacrifice and inconvenience. But the public pressure, through organizations something like the coalition, had the government running scared. It was going to go to the people, so the government said: "We will tell them how to operate." Then, what was the next thing? The government brought in Bill C-12. That was months ago. Members should differentiate between the various opinions or comments being made by public figures, and any notice of intention to amend the acts by means of bills to come before the House of Commons. The impending change has to do with the indexation part. It goes on to say:
There are several pension studies in progress now, some federal and some provincial, relating to the over-all subject of pensions in Canada, with particular reference to comparisons between public service and private sector pensions, and including the Canada Pension Plan. The public service pension plan is a part of this over-all debate, and the subject is complex, not only in terms of the above noted comparison, but also in terms of what pension benefits should exist for Canadian citizens as a basic expectation. A part of these discussions lies in settling the basic question of whether private sector pensions should be upgraded, essentially to give broad comparability with public service pensions, or whether public service pensions should be downgraded to give broad comparability with private sector pensions.
As I said before, and I have no hesitation or any equivocation whatsoever, this government-and I notice Mr. Speaker is nodding his head in the affirmative-has gone about bashing

the public service. I asked a question of the then president of the treasury board on January 30, 1978. I asked whether it would be on an ad hoc basis or in what form they would bring it in light of the Tomenson-Alexander study. I read the reply from the then president of the treasury board:
Our position will require a great deal of analysis and thought. We have a commitment to consult with the bargaining agents and the advisory committee on public service pensions.

speechtext:
I hear the ha, ha! All I know is the bill was not introduced and the government did not get it before Christmas. I do not know whether it will get it before April. With all due respect to the President of the Treasury Board, he has not told us a doggone thing. The questions we have are exemplified by those on the order paper. I hope the President of the Treasury Board realizes we have a lot of work to do before we even start on clause 1.
We have come a long way from the days when pensions first appeared and were viewed as a reward for long and faithful service. Pensions are no longer a reward but a form of deferred compensation. They are no longer a privilege but a right.
I am glad the minister has indicated that he appreciates the fact that those in the $7,000 and $8,000 bracket make up 95 per cent of those about whom we are talking. We are talking of those at the bottom of the economic ladder.
One of the major problems that currently exists is the remarkably uneven nature of the changes that have occurred. Some persons must rely on CPP, OAS or QPP. Others have additional pensions. Some even have indexed pensions. This unevenness has created the current pension debate.
Accordingly, we should also direct our attention to the 60 per cent of the labour force that does not belong to any private pension plan and must rely on CPP, OAS and so on, and those who make private pension plan contributions but collect no benefits as a result of the problems of portability and so on. We must, as well, be concerned about mechanisms to allow the private sector to offer indexed pensions more easily. Therefore, that must be investigated. That is why I listed the many witnesses who would be able to give us that expertise.
What disturbs me is why we are having this debate now. I remember the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) going around this country and walking in and out of this House of Commons talking about how inflation had been licked, how it had been wrestled to the ground. Neither became a reality. We have inflation of about 8.5 per cent. I understand it is going to get worse. Even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) does not know what it will be. He has upped his November figure from 6.5 to 7.5 per cent. He does not know what is going on.
When government ministers brought in wage and price controls, or whatever they called it, their incomes policy, they told the Canadian people it would be down to 4 per cent by 1978. If they had done their job in terms of cutting government spending, we may have been closer to that figure. If they had stopped printing money, we would have been closer. However, they did not do that. They kept on printing money and spending. Not only that, but they continued to waste money. I need only refer to the Auditor General's condemnation regarding the government's management of fiscal and monetary policy. Therefore, inflation just took off.
We are nowhere near 4 per cent, and all economic indicators point to the situation getting tougher. Even the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada have implied that, although the minister likes to say that the situation looks great. He knows it is not great. We have 1,250,000 people out
February 8, 1979

of work, and he is trying to con me? I have been around too long.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
A lot of Canadians just do not accept that nonsense. As a result of not reaching that 4 per cent which was guaranteed by the government, they have had to ask Canadians to trust them. They do this even though they flip-flop. They deceived the Canadian people during the 1974 election. At that time they said wage and price controls would not work. They said they did not work in Great Britain and in the United States and, under no circumstances, would they freeze wages.
People therefore became concerned about the form, extent, and cost of indexing in the public sector. Because of government incompetence and mismanagement, the alleged uneve-ness and inequity became more worrisome, bothersome, and frustrating.
It is necessary to go into the history of indexed pensions in order that we be better advised as to the background and what must be done for the future. Before 1970, the pension benefits of retired public servants in Canada were adjusted on an ad hoc basis. The persistent and relatively high levels of inflation in the late sixties led the federal government to review its policy. An advisory committee on the Public Service Superannuation Act examined various proposals for a special contributory plan and concluded that such a plan, financed by equal contributions of the government's employees, was feasible. The objective of the plan was to finance the cost of partially protecting the value of the government sponsored retirement and other benefits to the public service on a continuing basis.
An act to provide supplementary retirement benefits to certain persons in receipt of pensions from the Consolidated Revenue Fund was adopted in 1970. It provided that, commencing in the month of April, 1970, a supplementary retirement benefit would be paid to every recipient of pension, the amount of benefit to be calculated by means of a particular formula. The maximum supplementary benefit payable to public servants was tied to the indexation of the Canada Pension Plan as it read on January 1, 1970.
The benefit index of the supplementary pension plan was connected to the pension index of the Canada Pension Plan. The latter act defined the pension index as the average of the consumer price index for Canada as published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, as it then was, under the authority of the Statistics of Canada Act, for each month in a 12-month period ending June 30 in the preceding year or 1.02 times the pension index of the preceding year, whichever was less. In this way supplementary pension benefits of public servants were partially indexed to the cost of living, but only partially because the maximum supplementary benefit was limited to 2 per cent of the basic pension of the preceding year. The supplementary retirement benefit for public servants would be financed equally by the government and by the employee, each
Pensions
contributing half a per cent of gross salary to a special fund out of which payment would be made.
The 2 per cent limit to pension increases was eliminated by the Statute Law Supplementary Retirement Benefits Amendment Act, 1973, and the amendment substituted a new definition for pension index. I will quote it:
Pension index with respect to any year means the average for that year of the consumer price index for Canada as published by Statistics Canada for each month of the 12-month period ending on the 30th day of September in the immediately preceding year.
Accordingly, any increase in the consumer price index would be fully reflected in escalation of benefits under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. I think it is important that this should be put on record.
Introducing the amendment to the House at the time, the Hon. C. M. Drury noted that the government had agreed to assume the cost of all escalation for all those who had retired before 1970 and, the balance of the cost of the escalation of pensions of persons retired since 1969, which had not been covered by matching contributions made by those persons and by the government in respect to them. Aside from this, the government intended to adhere to the principle of equal employer/employee contributions. Initially, this would increase the cost to both of providing the supplementary benefits from one half of 1 per cent to 1 per cent of gross salary, with a strong likelihood of future increases. As a matter of fact, the position of the government of the day at that time was, and I quote:
In the long run the contribution of half of one per cent together with the government's matching contribution would almost certainly be insufficient to cover the cost of escalation for employees entering the public service with an average working life of 30 years in the service ahead of them. There is an assumption that it would be necessary to increase the contribution made in the very near future if, such an employee is to pay half the cost of his pension escalation after retirement. The assumption is that it would not be necessary to do so for a few years. The government is proposing to adopt a phased approach under which the present rate of contribution is to be raised by half of one per cent each effective January 1, 1977. What further increases might be required in later years will be determined by future parliaments.
I want to pause here to say that a public servant, a top level public servant with a high rank in the armed forces, called me to ask why, if it was thought the program was in trouble, the government had not asked the employees to pay a further one half per cent. I said I did not know. A moment ago I heard the hon. member for Ottawa West say it was not needed. 1 am simply throwing out the question. Why all this rigmarole? Why all the complexity? Why this frustration and uncertainty? At that time the basic reaction of the opposition to the legislation was that it was long overdue and not enough.
Rather than question a provision which was generally unavailable in private enterprise, a number of opposition members advocated indexing public service pensions to a wages and salaries index, or to an index based on the gross national product, much more expensive options than indexation to the consumer price index. I was here. Many members now in this Chamber were here. Most of us were here. But we really didn't know what was going on. We were conned in 1974 but we are not going to be conned again. I am not saying the minister has

February 8, 1979
Pensions
conned us. I am saying that what happened in 1974 led us to an impulsive conclusion. So we are now at the stage of full indexing.
It is no secret that the present provision of indexed pensions has, in recent years, come under increasing criticism from the general public and, of course, the public service is concerned about the attitude which the general public has expressed. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, we must get at the truth. Rightly or wrongly, the public perception is that the Public Service Superannuation Act in conjunction with the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act provides public servants with pensions which are among the best in the country. Essentially only large financial institutions are providing similar initial benefit levels. Exceptions exist at lower earnings levels for the very large industrial organizations.
Furthermore, on January 1 each year public service pensions are increased by the change in the consumer price index. Only about .6 per cent of workers in the private sector have pensions that are comparable. The increase on January 1, 1978, was 7.2 per cent. I am not too sure what it was on January 1, 1979, but we must always remember, Mr. Speaker, that there is a contribution by the public servant of 6.5 per cent of salary as a basic pension and one per cent for indexation, with matching done by the government.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to indicate just how pleased we were to hear what the minister had to say. I want to quote him again. He indicated what would have happened had Bill C-12 come into effect when they thought it would come into effect on January 1. I will read this out as a result of my House leader asking that extremely important question. This is what the minister indicated:
Basically our intent was to give full indexation for all pensionable incomes under $7,000, which I think amounts to something around 75 per cent or 80 per cent. Regarding amounts above $7,000, during the year 1979 we intend to index those at 8 per cent, in 1980 at 7 per cent and in 1981 at 6 per cent. 1 should point out, as hon. members will see when they look at the report from the chief actuary, that this was based on an inflation assumption of 8.8 per cent when in fact it turned out to be 8.4 per cent, so we are better off than we thought we would be. With a little good luck this provision hopefully will be even more generous for the years 1980, 1981 and 1982.
We now know that the ad hoc arrangement will not take effect until January 1, 1980. This does make a difference and we welcome that, but I do not think the minister had any choice. And I still have to think about the April 1 deadline which the minister wants to introduce. As well, there will be provisions he wants to bring in by proclamation. He is going to have to show us, though, why he did not go all the way with it and whether there are savings because in truth, Mr. Speaker, I do not trust the figures that this government throws out. Most of them come from the Minister of Finance and his department, and he's been wrong ever since I've been here with respect to growth, with respect to unemployment, with respect to inflation. We need, for example, other people to tell us what the inflation rate will be. We need other people to make guesses with respect to the wage rate and the interest rate. All of these things will have a bearing on this bill.

One of the major criticisms levelled against the indexing of public service pensions is that the current contribution rate- one per cent of salary by the employee and a matching contribution by the employer-is not sufficient to cover the cost of indexing when inflation rates run as high as they have in recent years. This is the issue.
A second major criticism of public service pensions relates to early retirement. Under the present system a person can retire with a fully indexed pension if years of age plus service equal 85. This system encourages those eligible to retire at the age of 55. Many of them have taken this option and have subsequently taken jobs with private industry, perhaps even as consultants selling their services to the government.
A third major criticism concerns a loophole in the existing legislation which allows a person who retires in December to collect a full year's indexing the following January.
This is what makes me so angry with the government. The Treasury Board initially reacted to the criticism of public service pensions by publishing in October, 1976, a brief about the basic facts on pensions in the public service in Canada. In this brief they attempted to prove that in the long run the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act would be sound. I want to quote from that document because some aspects of it have been forgotten. It is dated October 18, 1976, and is entitled "Basic Facts about Pensions in the Public Service of Canada". This is what is stated at the bottom of page 14:
In other words, employer pension costs for the federal public service are expected to be reasonably stable, as long as the relationships observed in the past between rates of inflation, interest and salary increase remain substantially the same. Even with continuing inflation at 8 per cent-an improbable hypothesis- financial requirements for the public service pension plan would not diverge significantly from past exjjerience if the normal long-term relationship between wages, interest and inflation were to be maintained.
On page 15 they give a couple of conclusions as follows:
The public service pension plan is financially sound. All basic pension payments-about 80 per cent of the total outlays recently-are financed on what actuaries call a fully funded basis, through employee and employer contributions. The remainder of outlays-indexation payments-are partially funded with the funded elements expected to increase gradually over the years.
Item number 6 on the same page reads:
New liabilities arising from the indexation of public servants' pensions are unlikely to increase the to;al pension costs of the government as a proportion of payroll. For one thing, the level of employee contributions to the indexation account is rising, and the average period of contribution is lengthening; for another, the basic features of the public service pension plan have been fairly stable, so that extra interest earnings might well be sufficient, in the 1980s, to meet actuarial deficiencies for basic pensions.
Perhaps that is what the hon. member for Ottawa West was talking about. But that was back in 1976. It was true then. That was the gospel, the bible. Now it is no longer the bible. That is why I say that I cannot trust this government.
On March 9, 1978, the Tomenson-Alexander report was tabled which points out that if the public service pension plan, including indexing, were placed on a fully funded basis, the plan, in addition to employee contributions, would require continuing government-employer contributions of 15.3 per
February 8, 1979

cent of the payroll for current service and would face an initial unfunded actuarial liability of $5.9 billion for past service, most of which arises from the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act.
We will have to find out whether that is true. I will not just accept that. They will have to tell us how they arrived at that conclusion, why they arrived at it and what are the solutions. The report further indicated that if the unfunded liability were amortized over 15 years, an additional employer contribution of 19.1 per cent of pay would have been required in 1976, decreasing to 5.2 per cent in 1990, and to zero thereafter.
Besides the funding problems, Tomenson-Alexander also compared the public service plan with the private sector and found that while 80 per cent of plans in the private sector have provided some post-retirement adjustments, averaging 66 per cent of the change in the CPI, only 5.8 per cent are covered by formal plan provisions, and only 0.6 per cent by full indexing provisions. The average annual employer contribution per employee in the private sector in 1975 was $676 compared to $1,020 under the PSSA and SRBA for the same period. Under full funding, the employer contribution under the PSSA and SRBA would be approximately $4,350 per participant. Further, they indicated that most private sector companies will be unwilling to grant open-ended indexing and will not want skilled employees to retire at age 55 as is possible in the federal public service.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, let me read from Hansard of March 9, 1978, at page 3634. As reported in Hansard, a question was raised with respect to the private sector. Now that we are dealing with the public sector, we should be concerned as well about the private sector. A Liberal member of parliament asked the then president of the Treasury Board the following question:
Does he have anything to say at this time about this other great concern with respect to indexed pensions, namely, the exemplary effect they might have on the private sector?
The then president of the treasury board indicated:
1 say quite candidly that they will have difficulties. It is one thing to say it is fair and just and should be done, but there is the other reality of the availability of funds and the method of paying for it. I cannot indicate to the hon. member yet what the findings of the Department of Finance and the Department of National Health and Welfare are, except that I hope they will be available very soon and will give some stimulation to the private sector.
It seems to me that the private sector cannot meet the standards set by this bill even at this time. I indicated earlier that the provinces are studying this problem, the federal government is studying it, and the Department of Finance is studying it. Everybody is studying the problem but no one has the answer. We still need mechanisms for the private sector. Where are the reports from the Minister of Finance and from the Department of National Health and Welfare?
In any event, the then president of the treasury board responded on March 9 by stating that the government would introduce legislation to amend the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. The purpose of the amendment would be to place a curb on some undesirable practices that have crept into the program, to close off some loopholes in the program, and to
Pensions
fortify the financial liability of the program against unexpected financial setbacks that could conceivably arise in the relatively distant future.
The government had also introduced legislation in the last session, a bill to deal with total compensation comparability, Bill C-28. I think that is all tied in together, and of course we must know what we are talking about when we talk about total compensation comparability because pensions and indexation of pensions are part and parcel of that.
I think it is necessary to summarize the contents of the bill. The major provisions of the bill are as follows. Pension indexing would no longer be automatically tied to the consumer price index but would be determined three years at a time on an ad hoc basis. If sufficient funds are not available for full CPI indexing, the pension increase would be based on the amount credited to the fund, based on employer and employee contributions as well as interest earnings. Over the next five years, indexing would be progressively deferred so that by 1983-I do not know what the date would be now-public service pensions would not be indexed until age 60, rather than at age 55 as is presently the case if the public servant has 30 years of service. A pensioner's first indexing adjustment would be prorated to the month of retirement, rather than paying the full adjustment in January, regardless of what month retirement occurs as is presently the case.
The proposed legislation would also establish the special pension program agreed to in 1976 by the government for air traffic controllers in operational or tower service, bringing them increased pension benefits. An additional 2 per cent of salary would be contributed by controllers and matched by the employer to pay for these benefits. The bill, which contains a number of technical amendments, also proposes that the government be permitted, as in the private sector, to amortize unfunded pension liabilities, in some instances over a 15-year period, instead of requiring that all unfunded public service pension liabilities be amortized over five years.
We have been waiting for 11 months for the government to present its detailed proposals on indexed pensions flowing out of the general principles and policies laid out last March 9 by the then president of the treasury board. During the debate which took place last March, I indicated on behalf of my party that we agreed with the government's intention to endorse a form of indexing if it was actuarially sound. That has always been the position of the Progressive Conservative party and still is our position. As a matter of fact, on May 4, Mr. C. L. Lockhart, president of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, was advised in writing as follows:
My party is committed to the principle of maintaining the purchasing power of pensions. We have been concerned that people on fixed incomes, particularly those living on small pensions, can least afford to be caught by inflation, for which they are not responsible.
The letter stated further:
However, protection against inflation must be achieved in a way that guaranteed an actuarially sound pension plan. The pension plan must be made to meet all future commitments to those who have made contributions and recognize the legitimate concerns of taxpayers.

But, even more important, the letter went on to say:
When specific legislation is introduced, my colleagues and I will work to ensure that there is full consultation with the public service on specific proposals.
The above views are those of my leader and are accepted by the members of the Progressive Conservative party. In my view, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt about the position of my leader and my party with respect to the principle of indexation. However, I went on to say in my March speech that while the Progressive Conservative party supports the government's broad intentions, support for its specific proposals will have to await the tabling of the bill itself. Of course the bill cannot spell out all of the day to day details on how these principles and policies will operate in individual and special situations. This is extremely important, and the minister just touched on it. The bill cannot ensure that the changeover to the new rules will be carried out in a smooth and equitable manner.
There will be other hon. members of my party who will address themselves to a specific concern regarding the armed forces and the RCMP. It will be necessary for my party to lay out in some detail the background information which parliament requires in order to arrive at an informed decision on the proposals contained in Bill C-12 in terms of costing and financial implications. Of course this will be done. Further, we will have something to say on the proposals related to air traffic controllers. We accept the thrust and direction, but the hearing of witnesses is important to determine if the government's provisionary ad hoc approach is feasible, just, and sound.
Let me say at the outset that my party wants to see all of the relevant facts and figures brought out in the open. When full indexing was established in 1974, clearly parliament was not provided with sufficient information. If it had been, we would not be back here this evening altering the formula which was put in place approximately five years ago. We do not believe it is right that a person's pension, which he believes he is paying for with every pay cheque, should be forever dependent upon the whim of future public and government opinion.
Parliament and the public service have a right to know, before the bill is passed, just how much indexing can be provided in the future, not just three years in the future, but 15, 20 and even 30 years in the future, when the bulk of public servants working today will be reaching retirement age. The government's calculations and assumptions should be a matter of public record before the bill is passed, so that public servants will know with some certainty to what extent their pensions will reflect changes in the CPI when they retire.
In his speech on March 9, the then president of the treasury board referred to the proposed changes by stating they:
-are designed to firm up the financial undertakings of the program to ensure that we are not stirring up future trouble for taxpayers and public service pensioners.
Indeed this bill must achieve that goal. The minister must make public the actuarial calculations which lead to that conclusion. It is inconceivable that the government would
(Mr. Alexander.]
introduce legislation, or that the House would be asked to approve legislation, without some idea of what will happen in the future. The type of information parliament requires will be spelled out more clearly by the hon. member for York-Scar-borough, who is an actuary. He knows a lot about this bill and what it means to have something actuarially sound. I hope the minister or his officials do not expect to con or bamboozle members on this side. We have a top flight man who understands figures and how they can be manipulated, the hon. member for York-Scarborough.

The Tomenson-Alexander report on indexed pensions tabled last March by the former minister recommended that an actuarial costing be undertaken and published before any major changes in the pension program are legislated. To my knowledge the minister has not given this information. Also, the report recommended that while the chief actuary might undertake the study, it should be reviewed by an independent group of three actuaries. We demand that the government provide parliament with this basic information, if it has not done so already.
On March 9 the then minister spoke of a desire to eliminate undesirable financial setbacks in the future. This is our concern also. We do not want to be back here in five years, or even 15 or 20 years, being asked once again to legislate possible reductions in public service pensions. We want to know now that this proposal is financially viable. We want to see the results of the actuarial costing recommended by Tomenson-Alexander. Indeed these results are crucial for the drafting of such legislation. We want to see the government's three-year projections, as well as its long-term ones. We want to put to rest once and for all the suspicions that this is a stop-gap measure, and that parliament might have to be called in to make further reductions in the future. We want the facts and figures necessary to give public servants some degree of satisfaction that these provisions will not lead to a situation where their pensions will be reduced drastically in the face of continuing inflation.
If there is a major problem with the bill, it relates to the decision to replace full CPI indexing with ad hoc adjustments to be made every three years. This provision requires that the President of the Treasury Board, with the advice of the chief actuary of the Department of Insurance, shall estimate the funds available for indexing in each three-year period. If the minister discovers there is not sufficient funds, he will advise the governor in council on the amount of indexing which should occur.
The problem is twofold in this regard. First, the minister can make this decision without seeking outside advice. Because of the number of actuarial assumptions which must be made, including an assumption about future interest rates, this gives a great deal of freedom to the minister. Slight changes in the assumptions can yield very different results. For instance, until last year when outside actuaries and accountants got into the act, the government was convinced there was not a problem with the indexing of public service pensions and, with appropriately chosen assumptions, it made it appear that there was no problem.
This leads to the second problem-the possibility the minister could use this provision for political purposes. The assumptions he chooses, and consequently the amount of funds available for indexing, could be quite different in an election year
Pensions
than in a non-election one. Accordingly we believe that amendments should be introduced to the bill. It should be ensured that the three-year actuarial valuation will be subject to review by independent actuaries as recommended by Tomenson-Alexander in its report. It should be ensured that any valuation will include long-term as well as short-term estimates. It should be ensured that any actuarial valuation and review are tabled in the House prior to October 31 for the purposes of the following three years.
My speech is somewhat lengthy because we are not going to have that many speakers. We are prepared to expedite the debate at second reading so that the bill can be sent to committee where it can be examined carefully, where expert witnesses, some of whom I mentioned earlier, may be called upon to give testimony, and where all facts can be brought out in the open. Also we will be asking for information about the proposals to deal with air traffic controllers which provide them with early retirement features at increased contribution rates. We will want to see actuarial valuations to support these proposals. Also we will raise questions concerning some of the technical amendments during committee hearings.
While the Progressive Conservative party is prepared to begin clause by clause study and hearing the witnesses, I must warn the government that future total support will depend upon the answers we receive in the days ahead. Sincerely we hope the facts and figures behind the bill will prove the bill accomplishes the stated goal of the minister to fortify the financial viability of public service pensions. Public servants should know with some degree of certainty that they are paying for and are entitled to receive pensions which reasonably reflect changes in the CPI, and that this will not impose any undue burden on the taxpayer.
At this time I should like to state that the provisions regarding air traffic controllers arise from an agreement reached in 1976 and are modelled after similar provisions in the United States. One provision deals with workers in control towers who work under stress. That is why I think you will be hearing from the armed services and the RCMP, because they also work under stress and at some risk. Accordingly, there was a certain provision made for control tower people. Under such circumstances regarding controllers, and if retaining or the obtaining of alternate employment fails, they could receive early pensions.
The provision provides for voluntary retirement at full pension at age 50 after 25 years' service in an air traffic control tower. If retirement is involuntary, it provides for an immediate pension based on the number of years of service after ten years, with no penalty at age 45 with 20 years. This will be financed by a 2 per cent increase in the contribution rate of air traffic controllers and a matching employer contribution.
There are a number of unanswered questions which must be answered regarding this bill. Tomenson-Alexander recommended that an actuarial valuation of the combined pension program be undertaken before any major changes are made.

Has the government undertaken any actuarial valuation of the combined plan? If so, what actuarial assumptions were used, what amount of indexing will be available to the public service, Canadian forces and RCMP in the three-year period from 1980 to 1982? What amount of indexing will be available in subsequent three-year periods?
The bill creates three separate funds for the public service, the armed forces and the RCMP out of which indexing will be paid based on an estimate of the funds available for each three-year period starting with 1980-82.
If estimates are too high in early years, could this lead to a situation where pensions will be reduced in the face of high inflation in later years? Will the amount of indexing for everybody coming under the SBRA be based on the calculation of funds available in the public service account? If so, is it not possible for one account to run out of money before the others? Alternatively, different groups might receive different amounts of indexing. Who will pay for any deficits? The bill proposes to transfer excess interest on the retired employee's share of the public service superannuation account to the supplementary retirement benefits account. What is the expected annual increase in cost to the government in respect of the public service superannuation account as a result of this decision? At present, the government credits interest to the accounts based on the interest rate on long-term government bonds. Will future interest rates be based on a more fair interest marker reflecting investment opportunities which would be available in the market? I think that is what the minister indicated. What asset mix will be used?
One of the greatest concerns with public service pensions relates to the problem resulting from phanton funding. In other words, all excess contributions each year go into consolidated revenue, and payments are made from consolidated revenue. There is in reality only a paper entry, not a real fund. Has the government considered actually investing part of the assets of the public service superannuation account in non-government securities and, if so, what portion of the funds is the government considering in this regard?

1 suppose this is one time when, if I suggested we call it ten o'clock, 1 might get unanimous agreement. However, this is a very serious issue and I am happy to speak briefly on it tonight with the understanding that I shall probably have to adjourn the debate at ten o'clock and continue when we get back to this bill next week.
There is one thought expressed by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) and by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), in which I thoroughly concur; with them 1 decry the campaign, and particularly the nature of it, which has been against the indexing of public service pensions.
There are or have been enlightened insurance executives like Sydney Jackson of the Manufacturers Life, and the late William Anderson of North American Life, who have realized that pensions are not pensions unless they are indexed, and that the private insurance industry must address itself to that problem. I earnestly hope, with that kind of enlightenment on the private side, we will move in the direction of winning for all people in Canada adequate pensions and the indexing of those pensions, instead of having to listen to a campaign against public servants such as we have experienced for quite a considerable period of time.
I have referred to enlightened insurance executives. I am afraid that the others, those who wage the kind of campaign that was exemplified in an advertisement in the papers today, must face the suspicion that in times of inflation insurance companies gain if the pensions are not indexed, because they do not have to pay any more, but they make a lot more money in the interest that they earn on the funds which have been entrusted to them. The three of us who have spoken thus far are agreed on this issue. We have no use for the campaign which has been waged against the indexing of civil service pensions.
It is not particularly relevant at this point in my remarks, but having mentioned a couple of names, there are a couple of others that I would like to mention favourably. We are well served in the Government and Parliament of Canada by our public servants, and I know that it is a bit unfair to single out any particular individuals, but 1 think it would not be inappropriate for me to say that in this field, the whole question of the indexing of pensions and many other aspects of pensions, we were well served for many years by Mr. Hart Clark and the staff that surrounded him, and we are being well served today by Mr. W. A. Kelm and his staff. 1 hope it is not inappropriate for me to say that with Mr. Kelm in the gallery. After all, he has been there several days waiting for this bill to get started, and at least he should get credit for that.
1 approach this subject as a firm believer in the right of older people, not only to have pensions for their retirement years, but also in their right to have those pensions keep up, at least, with the cost of living. I emphasize the words "at least". In my view that does not go far enough. The fact of the matter
Pensions
is that in their working years our people get a certain measure of the increase in productivity which takes place. They seek and have a right to seek wage and salary increases which bear some relation to the gross national product. It is not good enough to say to older people who have retired, "All we shall do for you is to make sure that your income will keep up to the cost of living so that at age 70, 75 or 80 you can buy the same basket of goods and services you were able to buy at the point when you retired."
The standard of living is increasing for everybody else in society, and one of the reasons for increased productivity is the contribution made by those older people. I hope the day will come when, instead of having to defend indexation in relation to the rise in the cost of living, we will be joined in the battle to get it improved so that it is based on the gross national product and therefore will enable retired people to enjoy their rights as full members of the Canadian family.
I suspect that members are getting used to, if not a little tired of, hearing me make personal references in these debates on pensions, but one of the facts of life is that I have been involved in this issue for a long time. I well remember that in 1944 I asked my first question about the pensions of retired civil servants. They were referred to as civil servants in those days, not public servants. I did so because some older persons who had been retired for a number of years came to see me at my home in Winnipeg and laid their plight before me. They convinced me that this was an issue that one should pursue, so I took it on in 1944. The members who were here a few years ago-there are no members here tonight who were here in 1944, the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) was here but does not happen to be present in the chamber tonight-will remember the many times during question period, in debate, and during the late show, when I pressed this issue.
One of the few times in this House when I found it difficult to speak was toward the end of 1969. It was 25 years after 1944, and I was able to stand up in this House to welcome the announcement made in December, 1969, by the then president of the treasury board, the Hon. C. M. Drury, that the escalation of the pensions of retired public servants would be put into effect. I sometimes tell that story to some of my younger colleagues who say they have been around here for a full term or a couple of terms and have not accomplished much yet. I say, "Stick around a while, some things take a quarter of a century." The reason for throwing in that personal reference is to make the point that I believe thoroughly in this, and the fact that it took such a long time to win it, and the fact that we won it, I think, gives a certain moral sanctity to it.
Along the way we won the beginnings of the escalation of other kinds of pensions. It was in the mid-1960s that we got the Canada Pension Plan which had in it a provision for indexing pensions up to a ceiling of 2 per cent. We began the indexing of old age pensions, again up to a ceiling of 2 per cent.
I was here, too, in the famous years from 1972 to 1974. They have been mentioned by other members tonight, but I

February 8, 1979
Adjournment Debate
would like to mention that those were the years of a minority parliament when we got those 2 per cent ceilings removed and got the indexing of public service pensions, RCMP pensions, Canadian Armed Forces pensions, old age security pensions, guaranteed income supplement pensions, pensions of veterans on disability payment, and so on, up to the full extent of the rise in the consumer price index.
I know that I have indulged in this bit of memory and reflection a number of times, and I make no apology for doing so because I think that the Parliament of Canada has been at its best when it has done these things to make life better for our older people. By mentioning those other pension plans to which I have referred, I emphasize that my concern-and I hope the concern of all members of this House-is not just for public servants but for all the people of Canada. Our job is not to backtrack on this program but to go ahead with it. I thoroughly dislike, and I decry, as the two previous speakers have, the campaigns of those who try to turn back the clock in so far as the indexing of pensions is concerned.
I take my stand along with the two persons I already named, my friend, the late Bill Anderson of North American life, and Sydney Jackson of Manufacturers Life, who realized the social responsibility of private industry and of the private insurance business to move into this field. That is what we should be doing, not having to cope with a campaign against the indexation of pensions, but moving in two directions; first to see to it that indexing applies to all pensions, public and private, and, second, to see to it that this indexing is made more in line with the rise in the standard of living and the rise in gross national product.
I will be happy to say more on this matter on Monday, or whenever we come back to Bill C-12. In the meantime, may I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT-CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE
ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT-CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight's debate arises from a question I put to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) two months ago. At that time I asked the Deputy Prime Minister what minister in his cabinet was going to put in place-like today-a new plan to arrest the current account deficit in this nation. The question was necessary because of the unsatisfactory answers received the day before from the super economic minister, sometimes known as the President of the Board of Economic Develop-

ment Ministers (Mr. Andras). That minister has simply said that the current account deficit was a problem of medium and long term and would have to be solved in that context. That is not good enough.
Unfortunately, the Deputy Prime Minister reiterated at that time that the problems were medium and long term, but gave no indication as to how to solve them. He did refer to the travel account deficit as being part of the problem and said that that problem was one which would have to be solved in a medium term sense.
The travel account deficit amounted to $1.8 billion last year compared with $29 million in 1968. Imagine, within ten years we shifted from a rather nominal deficit on the tourist account of $29 million to $1.8 billion last year, yet all the Deputy Prime Minister and the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers have to say is that that is a medium or long-term problem.
The fact is that the travel deficit alone represents 40 per cent of the current account deficit this year. Expressed another way, in the past four years the deficit on the travel account has represented $5.3 billion. Many authorities feel that that deficit may continue to increase. If we are looking for reasons why our diving dollar continues to dive lower and lower, we need look no further than the current account deficit of some $4.5 billion which we ran up last year.
Sometimes I feel that the government is unaware of the magnitude of what we are talking about. Let us look, for example, at what the Financial Post says in the current issue. It says that a foreign investment study in Florida has revealed that Canadians are the largest single group of foreign investors in that state. The study listed 45 Canadian controlled firms in land development in Florida and another 17 in which Canadians are partners. The reason I link the tourist deficit with the capital investment which is taking place in Florida is not just that the people are going down to sunny Florida as tourists; they are taking their money with them. They are investing Canadian dollars in that state in amounts which are estimated at $450 million at the present time, and it is anticipated that in the coming 15 years that amount will exceed $1.3 billion, yet here we have the Deputy Prime Minister and the superior economic minister opposite saying that this is a long-term or medium-term problem and, in effect, "Why bother with them?"
The magnitude of the travel account deficit, the interest and dividend deficit, and the resulting current account deficit, is that in the last five years we have actually had a total current account deficit of $18 billion. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) sometimes glibly says that we have always had that deficit. That is a straight misrepresentation. In the previous five years, the first five years if you like of this emperor's reign, there was a surplus. The surplus was something over $300 million per year, and yet here we have a government faced with a deficit of a current account nature for the last five years aggregating $18 billion and it has the audacity to tell us somehow that is a medium or long-term problem that it is not prepared to address at the present time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question put by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) on December 8. Let me begin by pointing out that historically Canada's balance of international payments has been characterized by a significant deficit on current account and a surplus on capital transactions.

speechtext: That is just not true, and you know it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT-CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE
speechtext:
Current account deficits for Canada are neither new, in fact they are the rule, not the exception, nor are they in themselves a bad thing. In order to finance high levels of capital formation and enhance economic growth, Canada has traditionally supplemented its domestic savings by recourse to foreign capital markets. Deficits on current account are the necessary counterpart of this.
Nevertheless, under present circumstances the government would view a reduction in Canada's current account deficit as a favourable development. We are optimistic that this will occur in the future. The deficit in the third quarter was influenced by some rather disappointing figures for Canada's international balance on merchandise trade in July and August. There are grounds for believing, however, that the merchandise trade figures for the summer months are not indicative of a trend. Taking a longer perspective, since the first quarter of 1976, we have experienced a substantial improvement in our merchandise trade account and we expect further gains. Our competitive position in international markets, which earlier had been a cause for concern, is much improved and this should exert a positive influence on our current account balance over the coming quarters.
In our view, as has been mentioned on many occasions, attempting to affect the pattern of Canada's international payments by artificial devices would be counterproductive and would be treating the symptoms rather than the causes of a problem. Effective adjustment in the balance of payments is best promoted by following sound macro-economic policies, not by taking ad hoc measures in reaction to erratic movements in reported data for a particular quarter.

By concentrating on the fundamental economic problems of the country, by maintaining control over the money supply, by slowing the rate of growth of government expenditures, and by promoting structural adjustments where needed we believe that we have laid the foundations for an improvement in our economic performance which will be reflected in a balance of payments structure appropriate to our situation.
Turning to the claim that the current account deficit is the reason behind the decline in the value of the Canadian dollar, surely this is an incomplete analysis. It completely ignores the role of capital account transactions, which, in Canada's case are of fundamental importance. I should point out, as well, that an examination of the historical record reveals that, on occasion, Canada has experienced simultaneously a current account deficit and a rising exchange rate.
Finally, with reference to the question on the expenditure of international reserves intervention in the foreign exchange market has been carried out with a view to maintaining orderly market conditions rather than defending any particular level for the exchange rate. During a period of adjustment in the balance of payments, intervention may be sizeable compared to a more tranquil period.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-USE OF EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTERS IN AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak with regard to a question I put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on Monday, February 5. I say at the start that the minister is guilty of a complete lack of concern for the safety of the flying public. He is arrogantly stupid. He is unwilling to act to safeguard the flying public. He is guilty of wilful and wanton misconduct in carrying out the duties of his office, and guilty of a cover-up that endangers the flying public. He is kamikaze minister. The difficulty is that he is not careless about his own life and safety, just the life and safety of everyone else who flies.
I will give the reasons why I say that. In 1975 the Department of Transport ordered private pilots to instal approved emergency locator transmitters on their aircraft. They had to have that completed by July 1, 1977. These ELTs or black boxes switch on automatically when a plane crashes. They then beam a powerful signal for up to 50 hours which enables

February 8, 1979
Adjournment Debate
rescuers in other aircraft to search and find them, even if they are completely hidden by trees, snow or whatever.
In October, 1977, the department ordered the complete removal of ELTs or ELT batteries from all aircraft. The reason was they had discovered that in two aircraft on the ground the lithium batteries which were used to power the ELTs had exploded, and that they might explode during flight. This, apparently, was due to a corrosion problem. If they corroded, they might explode.
That meant all aircraft, including the Churchill Falls jet, had to remove their ELTs. On December 9, 1977, when landing at Churchill Falls, the aircraft crashed about two miles short of the runway. There were two pilots and six passengers. It turned out subsequently that six of them died in the crash. The two who survived the crash died as a result to exposure to the cold.
The aircraft did not have an ELT. Two helicopters took off from Churchill Falls immediately. Because there was no ELT in the downed aircraft, and because it was snowing that evening, they could not find the aircraft. The aircraft was not found for two days. It was not discovered until December 11. The two survivors had frozen to death because they had not been discovered right away.
That was a bad mistake DOT made in ordering ELTs out of the aircraft, making a mandatory order that this be done. The Canadian Owners and Pilots Association says the department should have consulted with the industry and aircraft pilots and owners to find a quick solution to the problem. What they should have done was warned pilots and aircraft owners to check these lithium batteries and continually monitor them. It would be safer to have these ELTs on board, taking the small risk of the lithium battery exploding, something that would not happen if there was a constant check for corrosion.
In February, 1978, DOT changed its requirement and said that on a voluntary basis pilots could reinstate the ELT with a dry cell battery until a lithium battery was perfected. It is now a voluntary matter. That decision could have been made in October, 1977. If it had been on a voluntary basis on October, 1977, the CFL Co. aircraft would still have had the ELT and these two people probably would not have died due to exposure. Instead, it gave the order that they be all removed.
On Monday the minister confirmed to me that this is still voluntary. A year and some months later after this crash, aircraft are still not required to have ELTs on board, even the American type. All aircraft in the United States must have an ELT, but not here in Canada.
There was a magisterial inquiry into this crash which started in November in St. John's. Mr. H. Glynn-Reid of Moncton, chairman of the MOT operations group for air aviation safety, testified that the two who lived through the crash might have been found alive if the plane had been equipped with an ELT which would have given out automatic signals to aircraft. Another witness from MOT, Mr. W. R. Bowie, chairman of the flight recorder group, explained why the ELTs had been

removed. There were two cases where batteries exploded, though both aircraft were on the ground at the time.
I brought this matter up in the House. I was the first to reveal it publicly on August 23, and I have been campaigning about it ever since. The minister's department changed the report of the Accident Investigation Bureau, changed the report of the Safety Bureau and the Independent Review Board, changed the wording-something which I will not go into tonight-so that the report no longer clearly blamed the department for ordering those ELTs off the aircraft and so the minister, on November 6, had to tell the House that he had made it clear to officials that they could no longer change reports coming to them from the Safety Bureau or the Independent Accident Review Board. The minister has gone that far.
Then, further in the magisterial inquiry, giving evidence several days ago, Captain Powick, in charge of air search and rescue at Halifax, said he could not think of one dangerous incident involving ELTs in military aircraft. He said, further:
It is costing the taxpayer millions of dollars to search for aircraft which do not have ELT's on board. From my personal point of view I can see no reason not to have ELT's aboard the aircraft... sufficient time has elapsed to have found a suitable replacement (for the lithium battery).
All this illustrates the minister's complete disregard for the safety of the flying public. He shows no sense of urgency. More than a year after these incidents occurred they still have not found a battery. The reason the minister gives is that lithium batteries are not good in very cold weather. The weather in Canada is not always cold. If these batteries are good enough for the United States they are good enough for us, now.
The minister told us in this House on Monday that he could be "very assuring in terms of the performance of our airlines, our pilots and everyone operating the air travel system so Canadians need not be concerned." He said they need not be concerned about safety in the air, that Canadian safety levels are very high. Yet today there is a report in his department which says that air safety regulations are unco-ordinated and haphazard, that there is widespread ignorance and misunderstanding of the rules. A devastating indictment is contained in the report of his own department. Notwithstanding this, the minister comes to the House and makes misleading and false statements. I contend that he should resign immediately. As soon as that CFL Co. aircraft went down and it was discovered that there were two survivors who later died from exposure-

speechtext:
To respond to the hon. member's question, the airworthiness directive requiring the removal of all ELTs powered by lithium batteries is still in force. As the status report on this subject shows, replacement battery packs (with no lithium batteries) are now available for approximately 90 per cent of the current emergency locator transmitter systems in operation. Once all battery packs can be replaced, the original air navigation order calling for installation (where applicable) of a functioning ELT in aircraft will be back in force.
I am sure the hon. member is very much aware of the need for removing lithium batteries from aircraft. There are documented cases indicating the danger of using this type of battery for ELTs, although fortunately, there were no casualties in any of the reported cases. It was decided that lithium batteries used in ELTs presented an unacceptable high risk for use in civil aircraft. Therefore, an airworthiness directive was issued ordering their immediate removal.
In view of the serious situation arising from the removal of ELTs, and cognizant of the safety factors that guide our ELT policy, it has been the objective of the Canadian Air Transportation Administration to restore ELTs to service as quickly as possible.
There is evidence now that no alternate lithium based call would be available or proven safe for civil aircraft application in the immediate future. Consequently, the seven manufacturers of ELTs, who hold Canadian type approval, were formally asked to submit a proposal for a program to retrofit their manufactured ELTs with a substitute non-lithium battery. Five of these companies have received approval for a battery retrofit program. They represent about 90 per cent of the ELT population. There is the potential that the majority of ELTs will be returned to service over the period extending into later this year.
Returning ELTs to service represents an interim phase in upgrading their effectiveness. But it should be pointed out that the ELT system will be deficient in at least two areas during this interim period. The modified ELT with a non-lithium battery will not meet the operating requirements of minus 40 degrees centigrade for 100 hours. The ELTs prior to their
Adjournment Debate
removal from the civil aircraft fleet were experiencing numerous technical problems other than those involving their batteries. These deficiencies will continue to affect over-all ELT proficiency.
Operational efficiency of ELTs is a North American problem which has precipitated intense activity in the industry. Lead times required for research and development, regulatory change and implementation, mean that it will be some time before the desired high performance of the ELT system can be realized.

LOTTERIES-PROMOTION OF LOTO SELECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the question period on December 21, 1978, I asked two questions of the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo), in her capacity as minister of lotteries. As reported on pages 2344 and 2345 of Hansard I asked about the purchase and disbursement by Loto Canada of some $17,000 worth of foil-wrapped chocolate candies. I also asked why and at what cost an American author has been commissioned to write a book about Canadian lottery winners. Why an American author?
1 expect the parliamentary secretary will give full answers to these questions this evening. However, it was the closing assertion of the hon. lady which provoked me to call for this debate. She said:
Canadian lottery winners are extremely intelligent in their investment in Loto Canada because they are able to maintain most of their dollars in their bank accounts.
I am afraid I do not understand the minister's reference to "intelligent investment", but I certainly have to question the intelligence of the decision makers at Loto Canada. How did they ever blunder into this foolish and ill-fated Loto Select fiasco? The losses due to unfulfilled contracts could run as high as $37 million. Indeed, one has to question the competence of the minister in view of her scandalous mismanagement of this multimillion dollar adventure into the world of organized gambling.
Why was Loto Select terminal equipment for the "dollar a shot" lottery ordered in such great haste last June? Why was a $23 million contract placed for 2,000 slot machines from General Instrument Company of the United States? Why were tenders not called, recognizing that there were at least ten Canadian companies fully capable of supplying such equipment? Why, when this hypocritical government was spending tens of thousands of advertising dollars urging us to "buy Canadian", did it go to the United States? Why did the cabinet not seek the concurrence of the provinces and of parliament before embarking on this foolish project? Why has the minister consistently refused to explain this remarkable circumstance to the House of Commons?
In addition to the millions wasted on the leased lottery equipment, other millions were spent to renovate, furnish and equip two major data processing centres, one in Vancouver and the other in Montreal. I have visited the Vancouver facility,

February 8, 1979
Adjournment Debate
which occupies an entire floor of the Bordiguon building, about 10,000 square feet. The renovation cost was over $300,-
000.	Telephone trunk lines were brought in from all major cities in western Canada, costing about $1 million. A five year lease for the premises, at $9,000 per month, cannot be broken until next August, when a penalty of six months' rent amounting to $54,000 will have to be paid. Today, the Vancouver facility sits vacant except for more than $200,000 worth of furnishings now being sold off.
Over 50 employees were hired. They worked at Loto Select for only a few weeks. Each is receiving a severance allowance of about $10,000. At least one employee is back at his previous job, having picked up $10,000 in compensation without ever reporting for work with Loto Select.
The hon. minister regularly insists that Loto Canada plays a major role in supporting amateur sport in Canada. But what has Loto Canada really provided to the benefit of amateur sport? In 1977 the lottery took in $225 million, of which only $3.7 million or 1.6 per cent went directly to promote fitness and amateur sport. That is about 17 cents per capita. Of the balance, $25 million went to advertising and promotion, with the remainder going to wholesalers' commissions, prize money, and the Olympic debt.
It is high time for us to undertake a reassessment of the role and impact of Loto Canada. Does gambling organized by the state represent a veiled form of taxation which appeals most to those who can least afford to "play the games"? Those lower income Canadians who are more inclined to take a chance on the "big jack pot" are often those who impose the greatest burden on our social welfare systems. Personally I believe the federal government's involvement in lotteries is unnecessary, improper, and serves only to create a distorted sense of values, especially among our young people. Also it diverts the talents and energies of government ministers, such as the hon. lady, from the many really important problems which should be attended to in Canada today. I am pleased to see that at least two members on the government benches share my view, as expressed in the motion under Standing Order 43 moved last Friday by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) and seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni).
